items.body: Listening to Crude Walnut Taste, it is tempting to focus on Giorgi Koberidze‘s compositional rigour: the electroacoustic transformations, the dialogue with Western classical forms, the microscopic attention paid to the behaviour of sound. Those elements are certainly there, but they risk obscuring something equally important. This is a remarkably funny album. After all, the opening track, “Horsing Around”, gives the game away immediately. Crude Walnut Taste is not funny in the sense of parody or quotation, but in the pleasure it takes in constantly wrong-footing the listener who might be expecting an academic work. A gesture suddenly changes direction, a rhythmic idea gathers momentum before being interrupted by an entirely different line of thought. Titles such as “Quasi Sonata-Allegro”, “Experimental, electro-accoustic, spatial audio, Georgian, sound design, Tbilisi, ambient – Adagio” and “Tbilisian Faux-Valse” gesture towards familiar classical forms, but only long enough for Koberidze to dismantle them. As the composer explains in the accompanying interview, these references belong to an earlier period of his practice, when his relationship with classical composition was more direct and, in his own words, more “primitive”. And this is the paradox at the heart of the album. On the one hand it sounds almost primitive, built from raw acoustic matter; on the other, the speed with which ideas appear, collide and disappear constantly propels it forward. Without resorting to the tired label of “retro-futurism”, the image that kept returning while I listened was Georgiy Daneliya’s Kin-dza-dza!. The 1986 Soviet science-fiction comedy follows two ordinary citizens transported to a distant galaxy where advanced civilisation appears to have regressed into something primitive. The film was, of course, scored by the late Georgian composer Giya Kancheli, yet there is a comparable measure of irony and lightness of touch running through both works. That playfulness extends to the sound world itself. Much of the album is constructed from recordings of the doli, the Georgian drum, chosen precisely because it carries no melodic baggage. Rather than treating the instrument as a symbol of national identity, Koberidze breaks it down into tiny fragments that become the raw material for an unexpectedly broad range of textures. The result is music that remains unmistakably physical. Even the electronics rarely transform those sounds outright. However, what remains most surprising, is the album’s speed, and not just its manic kinetic energy, but also the speed with which ideas appear only to mutate. Very little is allowed to settle. Musical thoughts collide with a kind of controlled frenzy that recalls someone thinking faster than they can speak. And yet, despite this restless surface, the music never feels erratic. It remains playful without becoming flippant, rigorous without turning solemn. That is a rare balance, and one that gives Crude Walnut Taste its distinctive character. To help us crack the walnut, we approached Giorgi Koberidze directly. Crude Walnut Taste began life as a 20-channel spatial work commissioned for MONOM’s 4D Sound system before being reimagined in stereo for this release. How did the process of translating such a physically immersive piece into a two-channel format affect your relationship to the material? Were there aspects of the original spatial architecture that had to be sacrificed, or did the reduction reveal new details that were previously hidden? I actually already knew how the piece would sound in stereo, because I don’t have a twenty-channel speaker setup at my studio. So while working on it, I was composing in stereo from the start, imagining what sound could fit where. We then spent two weeks at MONOM Studio in Berlin, where we had the chance to rearrange the piece, add things, and sometimes exclude things, but the core idea of the music was already written in stereo, and that’s what made it possible to translate the twenty-channel piece back down. Of course, a lot is lost in that reduction, but the core idea is still there. It works almost the same as watching an IMAX film in a normal movie theatre: whatever really matters stays in focus, stays at the centre. What the IMAX size gives you additionally is maybe more air, more space, something that isn’t crucial to understanding the film itself. I’d say it’s the same with this piece: what really matters is still there in stereo. The MONOM system just gives more space and some additional ideas, but I wouldn’t say the piece is focused only on those twenty channels. Generally, my belief is that good music can be played on a single-string guitar, even if it was written for a hundred-channel system, as long as the idea itself is strong, and as long as the music matters more than the form. If we’re not talking about a piece where form is more important than the music, then I think it’s easily translatable anywhere. Across Forests, Tales, Cities, Forests, its Epilogue, and now Crude Walnut Taste, the doli seems to occupy an increasingly central role in your work. On this album, the instrument is extensively sampled, dissected and reconstructed through micro-editing techniques. What drew you to the doli as the primary sonic source, and how did transforming it electronically alter your perception of an instrument so deeply embedded in Georgian musical culture? I use the doli because it has no pitch. My problem with using tonal instruments from the Caucasus – the duduk, say, or the chuniri – is that they come with already-written melodies and harmonies, and I find it very hard to know how to use that material in modern music. At some point I decided I would never touch existing melody or harmony, because it’s already there, it’s already enough. It doesn’t need anything from me, or from anyone, to be transformed. The doli is interesting because you can use it without ever touching a melody or a harmony, it gives you a lot of possibility to take micro-material from it instead. But anyone who understands sound and sound design knows that, basically, you can turn any sound into anything. The instrument you choose is just a source for material, and from there you can go anywhere; it’s really about what physical material you’re comfortable working with. In my case, it’s the doli simply because it’s here – you’re in Georgia, there are dolis everywhere, you can just grab one. Also, the quality of that sound already carries something very familiar to every Georgian. By using it, you’re lightly touching this historical heritage, but it doesn’t give you licence to overuse it – to base your music on something already precious to Georgians and then claim it as your own. Some people use old melodies, traditional melodies especially, and I’m not against using old pop music in modern work. But when it comes to traditional music, it’s more delicate. So even when we do use tonal instruments like the duduk, we’re very careful never to cross into an already-written melody from Georgian folk music. Earlier works such as Forests, Tales, Cities, Forests felt almost cartographic, mapping landscapes, memories and imagined geographies through graphic scores, ensembles and field recordings. Crude Walnut Taste seems more focused on texture, gesture and acoustic matter itself. Do you see this album as a departure from those narrative and spatial concerns, or as another way of exploring the relationship between place, memory and sound? Also, several track titles—”Tbilisian Faux-Valse”, “Quasi Sonata-Allegro”, “Experimental, electro-accoustic, spatial audio, Georgian, sound design, Tbilisi, ambient – Adagio”—appear to reference established musical forms, yet the music itself constantly undermines expectations through fragmentation, electroacoustic processing and playful subversion. To what extent are these titles intended as affectionate dialogues with classical traditions, and how important is humour or irony within your compositional practice? First, some context: Crude Walnut Taste was actually written much earlier than Forests, Tales, Cities, Forests – about five years earlier. What the two albums share is a certain playfulness with, and closeness to, classical music. In 2019, when I wrote Crude Walnut Taste, I was a much younger student of classical composition, so the way I integrated that knowledge into the album was more direct, less hidden, even a bit more “primitive” – the melodic and harmonic moments lean more overtly classical. That’s also where the track titles come from, which I actually chose later, closer to the album’s release: names like “Tbilisian Faux-Valse” or “Quasi Sonata-Allegro.” They’re not literal sonata-allegros or waltzes, of course, but the mood and the harmonic gestures really are drawn from there. Looking back, I wouldn’t use these references so directly today – in Forests, Tales, Cities, Forests, similar techniques are used much more hidden, on a deeper, more background level. So, from that perspective, this earlier album carries a bit of irony, a bit of humour, and that’s something I’m quite fond of. I’ve always wanted to find a way to put humour inside music – it’s genuinely hard to do. My friend and musical collaborator Luka, the other half of Awwwaea, always used to come up with wonderfully funny musical ideas; I was constantly amazed at how he could make our whole friend group laugh for hours over a single musical idea. I’d say this album carries a little of that same spirit. At the same time, it’s a very personal record. Even the title comes from childhood: crude walnut taste refers to eating very raw, unripe walnuts as kids – cracking them open with your fingers while they’re still green, watching your fingers turn green and then black from the juice. That taste takes me straight back to those childhood memories: sometimes fast, sometimes a little sad, but mostly very bright, full of colourful images and imagination – but still raw, because the sounds themselves are raw. After I finished the album, a friend told me at a small concert that it felt like “music made for sounds no one else is using.” I loved that description, because the sounds you hear really are raw – almost taken straight from the computer as they are, with very little additional sound design or processing layered on top. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Review by kenethlevine — The passage of 30 years and a (duh, this is Polish neo prog after all) different vocalist notwithstanding, this reminds me of COLLAGE's classic "Moonshine" album, the one that still dwarfs most of the British giants. The problem is, it recalls the excesses of that masterpiece rather than its massive triumphs that inspired so much more from that country and beyond. Apparently conceived to lighten the mood amongst the lyrically downbeat sentiments of the reunion album "Over and Out" and to accompany it on the tour, "One and Only" should have been patterned after the sumptuous "Living in the Moonlight" rather than the bloated "In Your Eyes", which indeed means it's pretty good for the first half and abysmal for the home stretch. In the end, for a presumably lighter number, it's one of their most oppressive songs and I'd rather bathe in the tears of "What about the Pain (a family album)" a thousand times before I hear this again.

items.body: Review by arcane-beautiful — Terrifying Angels by Pure Reason Revolution sees the band making their darkest and heaviest album to date, but still keeping specific musical quirks that the band are known for. Taking their new prog sound into elements that include dark ambient, nu metal, psychedelic, symphonic and alternative rock, it proves that Jon Courtney's project still has heavy weight and impression. The trade off of vocals between Courtney & Annicke Shireen are mixed perfectly, with great depth and tone, while musically the band explore all aspects of their sound, making this a true stand out in their discography. While the longer tracks are the true attention grabbers, the shorter songs do keep to their more classic sound with heavier elements. I'd give this a low to mid 8 out of 10. The track I'd recommend is Terrifying Angels.

items.body: Review by alainPP — Kimmo P'RSTI's fourth album is a symphonic folk-prog-country affair featuring inspiring guest appearances, an analog sound, and Kimmo battling AI. His style ranges from Genesis and Yes to Supertramp, Camel, and Caravan."Circle of Wagons" showcases a distinctive folk-prog universe, a medieval touch in neo-classical mode, and a solemn sound reminiscent of Camel'it's a given. The choir, the melody that evokes Unitopia, the Archangel, and the cinematic drift on the famous "Close Encounters of the Third Kind" are all present. The guitar solo adds a touch of nostalgia to the repetitive melody, and the outro flute hints at the arrival of the alien. "Carousel" features fruity guitar, swirling keyboards, and a vintage instrumental that flirts with the "dinosaur" aesthetic, a tribute to JP Boffo. "Nightmares Come to Consume" features a fruity and catchy saxophone riff, reminiscent of PANZERPAPPA, but with a touch more Phil COLLINS. The shunt is a highlight, while the chorus becomes repetitive. "Chasing Echoes" has an airy, western-tinged melancholy feel, with a melting intro that perfectly captures the current mood. The vintage organ amplifies the effect of this beautiful, plaintive ballad, with vocals provided by one of the four regular members on this otherwise conventional track. "Things Not Seen" has the sound of a CAMEL album; Risto's saxophone brightens the air, the symphonic keyboard drift flirts with TANGERINE DREAM, followed by a blazing guitar solo and a prominent bassline that grabs your attention. The track is a versatile, danceable pop gem."In My Life" follows in the same vein, with a guitar solo and a raspy vocal that amplify the depth of this AMBROSIA track. "Light of Other Days" opens with a 100% bucolic feel, featuring an enchanting marshmallow flute followed by a devastating pad. The mysterious keyboard draws the listener in; the perfect instrumental that takes you on a journey of no return. "You and the Sun" begins with a jazzy keyboard, followed by a dynamic atmosphere with a prog-metal riff. The vocals of one of the four guests might surprise with their diversity, their distinctiveness, I mean. The mid-track shift evokes "Canterbury" sounds, reminiscent of CARAVAN, with this delicate, understated, soulless yet meticulously crafted variation. "Over the Sleeping Stars" begins with a vibrant bassline and rhythmic percussion on Risto's saxophone. The guitar leads into a fresh, energetic, and catchy instrumental. A festive folk-jazzy vibe at the start, the guitar solo ignites the music; simple, effective, the outro too short to send you soaring into space. "Only One in the Crowd" is a jazz-rock track featuring bass and distinctive keyboards; the vocals add a prog edge. You have to wait for the transitions to truly appreciate the progressive influences, particularly the delicate keyboard solo. The brooding vocals lead into a bluesy guitar solo that we adore, the high notes keeping us on the edge of our seats. This is the album's highlight, showcasing masterful playing. "With a Breath, I Linger" begins with a pastoral flute over a minimalist piano chord. A slow, solemn, almost martial melody, with Hanna and Rafael at the helm, is the perfect way to close this album of concentrated musical notes.Kimmo P'RSTI is the same artist who played in SAMURAI OF PROG, THE GUILDMASTER, and also contributed to Rafael PACHA.

items.body: Review by brainsuccasurgery — Vitelli has always had a well-stocked address book, including even a few living legends of '70s prog (Anthony Phillips, Tony Pagliuca, and David Cross, to name just a few, have contributed to Ellesmere's previous albums). This even allowed him to bring together no fewer than five exceptional guitarists in 2018 for *From Sea And Beyond* (Alan Benjamin, Trey Gunn, Keith More, Davy O'List, and Brett Kull, no less). On *Stranger Skies*, the lineup of prestigious guests continues. Surrounding the core lineup of Vitelli on bass and keyboards, Giacomo Anselmi (Goblin Rebirth) on electric guitars, Stefano Vicarelli (Fonderia) on Moog and Mellotron, and Mattias Olsson (who needs no introduction)?a master of odd time signatures and off-beat rhythms, who once again brings his crisp, precise, and creative drumming, the band brings together a few musicians?whom, like Olsson, we're tempted to leave unintroduced?including figures from prog of yesterday and today (Clive Nolan, Tomas Bodin, Riccardo Romano), well-known veterans (John Hackett, David Jackson), and others less so, such as Graeme Taylor (one of Gryphon's leaders) or Bob Hodges (Czar).Ellesmere's previous albums were mostly instrumental, featuring occasional guest vocalists (we recall Robert Berry's performance on *From Sea And Beyond*, though perhaps less so that of Luciano Regoli, the leader of Raccomandata Ricevuta Ritorno, an old RPI band) Here, it's the opposite: one and the same voice throughout, that of the remarkable and much-talked-about John Wilkinson. As the lead singer of the Liverpool band The Swan Chorus (with two albums to their credit, one released in 2018 and the other in 2023) and a member of Mama?which, as its name suggests, is a band that covers songs from Genesis's Phil Collins era?John brings a vocal tone so close to Collins's that it's almost uncanny. John Wilkinson can also be heard on a few tracks from the recent Samurai of Prog releases, such as "Like An Endless Sea" from Bernard & P�rsti's *Robinson Crusoe*.With the relative resurgence of the vinyl market offering an opportunity to make a little extra money, some progressive artists don't hesitate to shorten the length of their CDs and organize them into Side A and Side B, with an eye toward a potential vinyl release. Recently, the Canadian band Monarch Trail even titled their new album *Four Sides*, clearly signaling their intention to present it as a double album in the spirit of the golden age of the LP. Similarly, the first four tracks (totaling 23 minutes) of *Stranger Skies* are described as the "cold side" (meaning the more rock-oriented section), and the last two tracks?which are longer (totaling 24 minutes)?as the "hot side" (meaning more progressive). We'll see that it's not quite that simple.At the risk of sounding pedantic, let's dive right in with a track-by-track walkthrough of the album. Track #1, the first on Side A, known as the "cold" side: "Northwards" (6:50). After a majestic introduction in the classical symphonic style featuring Clive Nolan's keyboards, Ellesmere manages to revive?by blending them?the styles that Yes and Genesis had more or less adopted around 1977 (specifically, the tracks "Going For The One" and "Down And Out" as references): a multitrack sound, rich in effects and reverb, and a warm, full-bodied voice saturated with echo. Track #2: "Tundra" (6:43). Closer to early '80s Rush, especially in the chord arpeggios of a martial keyboard and the plump bass line characteristic of the Canadian band (it's no coincidence, by the way, that Vitelli's four-string Fender is named "Geddy Lee"!). A breathtaking fusion guitar solo closes out "Tundra" in the epic style of Dave Bainbridge. Track #3: "Crystallized," the only instrumental. In the intro, performed by Taylor, we catch a glimpse of the "Anthony Philips-style acoustic-pastoral" state of grace from the first album. It's a refreshing and welcome breather amid these intense three-quarters of an hour, with no downtime or let-up?which, paradoxically, might be the only criticism one could level at this album, provided you enjoy symphonic prog with unapologetic grandeur. The next track, a powerful neo-prog piece enhanced by David Jackson's unrestrained saxophone?which adds prog-fusion colors?is more in line with the rest of the album. Track #4: "Arctica" (4:16). The influence of Rush returns, with just as much energy and conviction but without the melodic clarity of the Toronto trio. A slight weak spot on *Stranger Skies*, despite the strength of the performance.Track #5, the first on Side B, known as the "hot" side: "Stranger Skies" (12:17). Closer to Steve Hackett's recent solo albums?his brother is once again on flute here?and less "edgy" than on *Wyrd*. John's vocals naturally seem to draw closer to those of Nad Sylvan. Along the way, one is also reminded of BBT or the most prog-oriented moments of Phil Collins' solo career. Track #6: "Another World" (11:43). We head in the direction of Arena, with Genesis from '78?'80 still in mind, particularly Rutherford's compositions. The final three minutes mark a complete break. Graceful and subtle, exquisite and imaginative, this finale?performed with delicacy by Tomas Bodin, which becomes obvious upon listening?is a lovely coda that stands in stark contrast to everything that came before.With musical themes more captivating than ever, greater cohesion than before, a consistent density that doesn't preclude fluidity, high-quality vocals, and a style a world away from the first album?closer to the subsequent ones while correcting their weaknesses or missteps but retaining their beautiful generosity? *Stranger Skies* is the most captivating of Roberto Vitelli's albums released under the name Ellesmere.

items.body: Review by CeeJayGee — I first discovered The Tangent 15 years ago, but it took me another couple of years to realise how good their music is. For a few years they were one of a handful of bands that I would call my favourites. The quality of the albums over the last few years has been so high that I would now say The Tangent is my favourite and most listened to band. I also appreciate being able to engage with Andie Tillison via social media. After I commented on the quality of this year's Po90 release, aftersometimelater, saying that it deserved to be more heavily marketed to raise its profile, Andie asked me whether I would like to hear some of the forthcoming album, Was. I jumped at the opportunity. I thought I would hear just a couple of tracks but over several weeks I was able to listen to and comment on the entire album. The album tells Andie's story through the music and the events that have shaped his own musical career. You could call it autobiographical. I don't believe anyone has attempted this previously and the purpose of the album has clearly inspired Andie to create some wonderful melodies.The first track I heard was the title track which I found immediately likeable and kept playing on repeat. I loved the simplicity of the riff which develops through the 22 minutes of the track. I couldn't stop playing it after the first listen. I then heard the Was Suite which at over 53 minutes is structured as six named segments that flow perfectly from one to another on the album. In classical music they would be called movements. When I first heard it, it was a single track. This is a largely instrumental piece and my past interest in classical music, and my love of rock and jazz fusion, makes this compulsive listening. The final segment, titled "Let Me Sing", is Andie sharing how he communicates through his music and his messages through poetic lyrics. It is a powerful conclusion which finishes with an inspirational speaker advising a young audience how to have good lives. I then heard Was Not, which Andie indicated to me was his favourite. This is another complex 20 minute plus and certainly matches Was and the Suite in terms of quality. The track opens with Andie's impressions of World War II formed from what he learned from the people who lived through and survived it, and the many films and TV series which his family watched together in his youth. I am a bit older than Andie, but I can empathise with this totally. The track develops with memories of further events and the hope that the World would learn from its past mistakes. He continues that the horrors we all see through the media seem to make us numb and he concludes with a very personal memory of his father in a nursing home. It is an extraordinary piece. The underlying themes and melodies are most enjoyable, but the piece is dominated by the message. For me, these are three standout pieces of music and these tracks are destined to be classics. The album also includes Follow The River plus four bonus tracks (two of which are around 20 minutes long) which are all enjoyable. I have little doubt that this will be my favourite 2026 album and it is likely to end up being my favourite album by The Tangent (so far).

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Logos channels a classic Gothic symphonic rock sound; the use of synthesizers and keyboards in "Origami in SOL" serves as an introduction to a complex musical tapestry reminiscent of Metamorfosi, particularly in "Paesaggi di insonnia," a track that borders on psychedelia through its juxtaposition of keyboard layers. The spirit of Genesis, combined with the saxophone, creates a dense atmosphere that nonetheless flows effortlessly, thanks to a dark, epic jazz influence, driven by a powerful underlying purpose: this is a concept album about the life of Sadako Sasaki. She was a Japanese girl who was two years old at the time of the nuclear attack on Hiroshima; she later fell ill and passed away at the age of twelve. This story gave rise to the Japanese legend of the thousand paper cranes (origami) that Sadako attempted to fold in the hope of recovering.The track's frenetic pace in Un lieto inquietarsi, is comparable to Le Orme's magnum opus, Felona e Sorona; the interplay between the drums, keyboards, and synthesizer weaves a musical tapestry that sets the stage for various solos, while an ominous aura gradually takes hold, including a decidedly non-festive use of the Hammond organ.Shifts in tempo occur naturally, amidst the abruptness with which the music bursts forth, drawing upon the full majesty of the classical repertoire, where Baroque polyphony paves the way for Luca Zerman's vocals, which adapt seamlessly to the context. In Il Sarto one notices the resemblance of Luca Zerman's voice to Aldo Tagliapietra (from Le Orme) and then he is joined by Elisa Montaldo, pianist and singer of the progressive band Il Tempio Delle Clessidre, in a great and emotional duet."Zaini di Elio" begins with the feel of 1970s Genesis, specifically the Phil Collins era, before allowing itself to be captivated by the structures of J.S. Bach; combined with Alessandro Perbellini's drumming, the music takes on the quality of a dance alongside the electric clavichord. It evokes Tony Banks and Phil Collins during the ...And Then There Were Three... period, though the sound drifts toward a more pastoral atmosphere, incorporating traditional vocal elements from the artist's native Verona. The layering of the various keyboard lines is so delicate that the transitions are imperceptible: it sounds as though the music had always been there.Sadako e le mille gru di cartareminds me of Hiroshima Mon Amour, Alain Resnais's film, and the subtlety of addressing such a subject with poetry and respect; stepping back to draw closer from a different angle, the kind of perspective only the passage of time can provide. Here, Claudio Antolini's piano takes on a new depth, and the rhythm that has driven the album pauses. Musical passages evoke Eastern melodies, telling the story through sound, accompanied by ghostly-sounding Minimoog emulations. Never before has a folded sheet, a crumpled scrap of paper, held so many layers of meaning or interpretation. The music provides the accompaniment: dramatic, yet also epic and inspiring, conveying a strength that rises from the ashes. Driven by keyboards and drums, the composition blends classical elements with syncopated rhythms, building toward an operatic finale as the paper figure unfolds, a symbol of the hope that nothing happens in vain, even if it seems otherwise at the time. That was precisely the hidden meaning behind the twists and intersections of the music itself.

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — For the most part early 70s German Krautrock morphed into the more instrumentally demanding Krautjazz fusion that found a rather sizable following in the second half of the decade when prog ingeneral had declined. Some bands though found a nice middle ground between the heady koschmischevibes of the space age and placed them alongside the more focused workouts of the jazz fusion scene.One such band was MORPHEUS that was spawned from an earlier band called Opossum which existed from1971 to 1975 but was never successful at releasing its own material although an archival releasewould see the light of day decades later in 2003. While Opossum was a more free form jazz kinda Kraut, a couple members wanted to play more psych-soaked structured tracks in the vein of other German fusion acts such as Kraan and Missus Beastleyor Embryo for that matter. The results was the short-lived MORPHEUS from Warburg that existed fortwo years from 1975 to 1977 and released its one and only album RABENTEUER smack dab in the middleof its career in 1976. Far from free form, MORPHEUS gathered grooves from the world of prog rock,trippy effects from the Kraut scene and more accessible jazz stylings also from the German scene.The result was a nicely displayed album that rocked, was smothered in jazz and offered a moresubdued heady vibe courtesy of spacey effects and a sensual flautist on board.Another of the many rarities that were generated during the era, RABENTEUER was limited to 500copies and went undiscovered until the Garden of Delights label resurrected the album for a 1998 CDrelease. Steeped in psych-fueled jazz rock, RABENTEUER features six all-instrumental tracks thatoffer funk-fueled bass grooves, gnarled workouts that offer labyrinthine structured compositions toflow around a rather accessible compositional flair only fortified with complex soundscapes,bountiful helpings of time signature deviations and ample doses of soloing between the variousmusicians that consisted of Peter Bl�meke (bass, flute), Gerold Adler (guitar), Heinrich Holtgreve(alto saxophone) and Alfred Franke (drums). While the tracks are primarily upbeat and more in thejazz rock camp, "Tanz Der Morphine" takes a dive into the space rock world of koschmische Kraut.Like many of the similarly minded bands of the era, MORPHEUS delivered the chops as far as jazz-infused prog was concerned with nice accessible hooks augmented by the more complex attributes ofthe words of both prog and fusion however the album as competently performed as it is sounds a bitlike those same similarly minded acts that didn't really add a lot to the world of jazz fusion atthis stage in the game. The tracks are pleasant but almost by the books in approach without any realfiery passion emerging by the rather consistent display of instrumental interplay. Overall it's anice supplemental piece from the era but not one that strikes me as utterly essential either.Pleasant but not much else. The CD version offers an extra long 20-minute jam track but this is evenof less interest than the album in general.3.5 rounded down

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — One of the many one and done acts that emerged in Germany's fertile Krautrock scene actually lastedfrom 1973 when it formed in Bottrop until the band folded in 1980. While only releasing one album,1975's BROKEN DOOR, the band went through many lineup changes with only one version of the bandmanaging to record and release something but even though a single album was recorded and set tovinyl, it was produced in such low numbers that it was virtually forgotten shortly after its releasealthough the band did frequent the live circuits for its entire run. Luckily BROKEN DOOR was rescuedby the Garden of Delights label and has emerged as one of those unexpected gems that was almostcompletely lost to history.With a rather contradictory band name juxtaposed to a disheartening album title, PROSPER wassomewhat unique and whereas some German prog was not Krautrock and not all Krautrock wasprogressive, PROSPER found the nice in-between zone that allowed the headier atmospheric texturesand spaciness of the koschmische sounds exist in full space rock mode all the while offering anabundance of virtuosic instrumental moments mostly courtesy of guitarist Evert Brettschneider whowas concurrently active in the jazz fusion group Contract Trio. Not surprisingly some of thisjazziness seeped into PROSPER which works surprisingly well. Add some King Crimson grit to the mixand you're in for a real treat with this one.The album is primarily instrumental dishing out a multitude of space rock-tinged motifs laced withmoments of progressive rock heft and jazzy accouterments. The band was a five-piece but implementeda diverse array of guitar tones (both acoustic and electric) as well as a plethora of keys rangingfrom the Fender Rhodes and Mini-Moog to mellotrons and other electronic effects however the thumpingbass grooves clearly point to Amon Dull II's heady mix of kosmische kraftiness. The album featuredeight tracks which range from softer contemplative space rock to more jazz-fueled prog. The opening"Beginning" offers a nice rotisserie of all the styles on the menu and elegantly passes the batonfrom one genre shift to another. The band's dexterity in handling the instrumentation allows thealbum to take on a more epic feel as opposed to many Kraut acts that were simply going for theescapist approach.While the album is fairly uniform in its feel, the mid-album clunker "Your Country" sounds woefullyout of place with its country rock style that wouldn't have sounded out of place on an album fromThe Band and although competently performed somewhat derails the momentum of the album's continuityhowever the surrounding material is strong enough to allow the listener to merely shrug it off assome kind of unfortunate anomaly. Overall PROSPER's debut release is indeed a true gem that took thebest aspects of the varying Krautrock and prog styles of the era and seamlessly agglutinated it allinto a cohesive sound of its own right. This is indeed a band that should've released another albumor two before evaporating into the 1980s but like many bands of the day, we're actually lucky toeven have the opportunity to experience this one once rare and unknown band's sole artifact.

items.body: Review by kenethlevine — Sometimes a rest is as good as a change. Having disbanded after the underwhelming "Lantaloon", DANDO SHAFT resurfaced for one 1977 album with all the principals still available, though Polly doesn't sing any lead at all and is almost just there for the credits. In the meantime, a few dignitaries help expand the credit list, namely ROD CLEMENTS of LINDISFARNE and DANNY THOMPSON of PENTANGLE both on bass, as well as a fledgling saxophonist Paul Dunmall who usurps the spotlight whether it's on him or not. But is it prog? And is it good? Yes. It's that rare comeback album from the late 1970s that pleasantly surprises. It asks the "what if" question or makes the "if only" statement , in this case, could this have changed the bands fortunes if released in 1973? The rock component, notably the bluesy electric guitars and percussions, are just one aspect that elevates this above DANDO's usual twee personae, with the violins fitting like a fiddle, illuminating the mastery of "Follow You", perhaps the group's best track, and "Feel Like I wanna go home". "Trees" marks the return of the olde Englishe and Celtic credentials, even more formidably on the sophisticated "Lady and Man", If it weren't for the preponderance of average albeit absolutely competent numbers, I could give this a roundup, but it's still a miniature triumph worthy of highness if not majesty.

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — Touted as the French female fronted version of Porcupine Tree, the Brittany based DELUSION SQUAREDemerged in 2009 as a band that delivered much more than being a mere Steven Wilson clone. A meretrio with a larger than life sound the band was initiated by bassist / keyboardist Emmanuel de SaintM�en and multi-instrumentalist Steven Francis who would hook up with guitarist and vocalist LorraineYoung and crank out a trilogy of sci-fi themed concept albums that explored all the good BladeRunner-esque dystopia and control systems of power structures. The band released three albums withYoung who would move on before the fourth and final release came out in 2018.The band's self-titled debut and first album of the trilogy delivered an album's worth of mindbending paranoia as it incorporates the story-telling narratives inspired by neo-prog acts such asPendragon, IQ and Arena although the alternative heavy rock guitar does indeed derive inspirationfrom the prog alt rock of Porcupine Tree's early 2000s works. The music while rooted in accessibleinstantly addictive melodies also offers a grunge-fueled guitar heft that gracefully melds theworlds of smooth atmospheric embellishments with a grittier guitar gusto. While the PT referencesget tossed around quite a bit, to my ears the band at this stage reminds me more of an accessiblecrossover version of Thinking Plague if that band had eschewed the jagged angularities of avant-progand focused more on pop hooks.The album of 11 tracks is nicely spanned out with interesting intros that introduces delicate piano-based hooks and tender, even fragile sounding vocals that contrast starkly with the alternative rockon the verge of becoming metal guitar chords and riffing sessions. On the production side the albumis both smoothly polished as well as offering a nice grating edge that keeps it on both sides of thefence simultaneously in a rather elegant fashion. The tracks vary sufficiently to keep the interestlevel up and although the album sounds a little generic with the opening "The Very Day," it doesn'ttake long for its charm to burrow into your psyche and let you acclimate rather quickly into thesubtle differences that point to varying influences but sound distant enough to offer a fresh spinon the more modern take on the alt heavy rock shtick.It's actually a very pleasant mix by merging the worlds of the hard alternative rock of PorcupineTree alone with the narrative layout of neo-prog acts along with the accompanying atmospheric andkeyboard prowess. Both aspects really hold up well and despite being only a trio, the members playmultiple instruments offering a much larger band sound. Add to that the Muse inspired topics ofconspiracy, crimes against humanity and secret projects and it doesn't take long to get sucked intothe mix of it all. While lyrics rarely appeal to me, i have say that DELUSION SQUARED's debutdelivered a nicely balanced album where themes, lyrics, instrumentation and production all cometogether in a unique yet familiar manner and performed quite well by the musicians without losingthat laid back charm even when rocking the house.

items.body: The funk Isaac Hayes and Willie Hutch wrote for American crime films in the early 1970s has a second home in Hamburg, a city whose funk scene runs through The Mighty Mocambos, Bacao Rhythm & Steel Band and the Légère Recordings label. The Winston Brothers come straight out of that scene, and “Get On Down” opens their second album, Sweets, out on 6 November via Ohio’s Colemine Records. It starts at full tempo: a hard breakbeat, choppy guitar chanks and a two-man horn section. Multi-instrumentalist and producer Sebastian Nagel and drummer Lucas Kochbeck formed the band as a school project, and Nagel describes the partnership in one line: “It’s a family thing, and we really know each other well.” Both play in Bacao, Nagel has also played with the Mocambos, and Kochbeck with Hamburg Spinners, part of a circuit where the same players keep turning up in each other’s line-ups. Sweets draws on that circuit, with Kimo Eiserbeck on saxophone and flute, Hans Stephan on trumpet and Carsten Meyer, the Hamburg keyboardist known as Erobique, on synths. Extra drums come from Max Weissenfeldt, once of Munich’s The Poets of Rhythm and now working as Max Whitefield. Sax and trumpet stick to short, angular stabs, the punctuating role horns play on the Hayes and Hutch scores. Midway the band drop into a dub-style section with delay on the instrumental parts, and the drums carry on underneath: like Drift, their 2022 debut, the track is built on the break. items.body: The Actions, a Bristol alt-electronic duo, released the single and video “Container” on 25 September 2026 through the Barcelona label No Where Records. The track is the first single from an album the duo have set for spring 2027, following their March 2026 single “Take More.” “Container” is also available to stream on Spotify. ‘Container’ marks The Actions’ first single since ‘Take More’ No Where Records describes “Container” as pushing the duo’s blend of “alternative electronics, dark textures and powerful songwriting” further than their previous single. The Actions describe themselves as an alt-electro-noise duo, and their recent work blends rock and electronic music with a punk-like directness, a shift they trace back to the March 2026 single “Take More.” About The Actions The Actions are a Bristol duo made up of Marta Argenio, who also performs as Silty, and Maurizio “Mo” Stellato. The pair share vocal, guitar and bass duties alongside electronics, exploring the space between rock and electronic music. Their debut album, “Flourish,” came out in 2021. The duo have previously opened for R.E.M., Green Day, Garbage and The Distillers, and earned airplay on BBC Radio 6 Music. The Actions returned in March 2026 with “Take More,” a three-track single pairing the original with a stripped-back “Flatland Mix” and a remix from IKO Twins, backed by a music video Mo edited through his own MStar Design work. The band said the record marked a turn toward something stronger and more direct than their earlier, more atmospheric work: “After our last, more transcendent record, we felt the urge to return with something stronger and more direct, and though it took time to get there, we knew this was the right moment to come back.” They called it “a song about growing up in the suburbs,” weighing whether to stay with the people they love or break away. The Actions joined No Where Records in July 2026. “Container” is the duo’s first release for the Barcelona label and the opening single from the album they have scheduled for spring 2027.

items.body: Then Comes Silence have reached a point where the more interesting question is no longer whether they have an identifiable sound, but what they are prepared to do with an identity that has become so clearly their own. Formed in Stockholm in 2012 and operating since 2022 as the trio of Alex Svenson, Hugo Zombie and Jonas Fransson, the band are now approaching their eighth album, “Requiem Ballroom,” due on 20 November 2026 via Metropolis Records. Conceived as a diptych, the record divides itself between Requiem and Ballroom, darkness and light, while recent singles “Judgement Day” and “Remaker Redeemer” have already begun to expose the contrast between those two halves. When I spoke with the band in 2024, our conversation touched on originality, conformity and the peculiar conservatism that can develop inside a scene supposedly built around difference. Two years later, those questions have become even more relevant. Rather than discussing “Requiem Ballroom” track by track, we returned to the larger tensions around it: how a band changes without performing reinvention for its own sake, when identity becomes formula, whether nostalgia can disguise itself as tradition, what happens when a trio becomes more focused by becoming smaller, and why sustaining a life in music may now be a harder problem than sustaining an artistic identity. Then Comes Silence interview Karo: When we spoke in 2024, Alex, you said the dark scene develops slowly and needs more originality. Two years later, Then Comes Silence are still immediately recognisable. How do you distinguish a strong identity from a language that has simply become comfortable? Alex: I still think the dark scene is developing very slowly. Can you honestly hear much of a difference between 2019 and 2026? The sound is basically the same, and most of the melodies still follow the same structures. I don’t know what others say about us, but I do think we distinguish ourselves from much of the scene by focusing more on the songs than on the sound. In that sense, we work in a rather traditional way: intro, verse, bridge and chorus. But who am I to judge? If people want to hear the same snare drum, synth pads and chorus-soaked guitars over and over again, maybe that’s what makes them feel good. I just know that we, Then Comes Silence, don’t really think that way. Karo: Your music has never depended on radical stylistic reinvention. Do you think artistic development can happen through changes in proportion, tension and emphasis rather than through introducing obviously new genres or sounds? Hugo: I think it can be a bit of everything you mention. We mix elements of different genres, such as that euro disco synth on “Judgement Day,” and this time we even tried new, exotic instruments in the recording. Both act as new ingredients in the Then Comes Silence sound. But just like a pizza, you can add different toppings and it will still be a pizza. Karo: “Requiem Ballroom” is built around opposites: darkness and light, ending and renewal. Yet Then Comes Silence have often been most interesting in the spaces between opposites: melody and severity, electronics and physical rock instrumentation, melancholy and momentum. Is the album’s binary structure something you actually believe in, or something you wanted to test and complicate? Alex: We believe in everything we do. There’s no theatre. This album is an experiment and a game. Team this vs team that. Karo: The two halves were mixed separately, by Tom van Heesch and Jon Bordon, but still have to exist as one Then Comes Silence record. Where does the identity of the band ultimately reside if the same material can be viewed through two different sonic perspectives? Hugo: The two halves were mixed separately, and recorded differently: different drums, amps, guitars. We wanted them both to have a distinct sound, but at the same time we didn’t want the album to feel like a compilation, so there’s still a sense of coherence between them. The identity of the band is there because it’s the same band using different approaches. Karo: Since becoming a trio, the band has sounded increasingly focused rather than reduced. Has having fewer people in the room actually widened the musical possibilities because the core identity became clearer? Hugo: It’s easier to work with a smaller team of totally focused people than a bigger team that includes distracted people with other priorities. That will only slow you down. Our roles in the band are totally clear; we are all focused on what we are doing, and that allows us to be more effective. Karo: You have now reached your eighth album. At this stage, is reinvention still a useful ambition, or does it become more interesting to understand more precisely what Then Comes Silence should never lose? Alex: We have been constantly active for years and haven’t really taken a break from each other or from music. The soul of Then Comes Silence will always stay the same, no matter how many times we reinvent ourselves. Karo: In our previous conversation, you spoke very positively about the Goth and Post-Punk community but also criticised its tendency towards conformity. Now that Then Comes Silence themselves are an established part of that scene, is it harder to criticise its conventions from the inside? Hugo: We all love the Goth and Post-Punk community. It’s our home. But I don’t think it matters how established you are; conformity will always be the enemy of creativity, which is meant to be at the core of this scene. For me, there are a lot of bands using the same formula, and it feels boring. But then again, others could think that we are doing the same, so in the end it doesn’t really matter. It’s just about what you enjoy listening to and what you don’t. Karo: You also mentioned then that younger audiences in the US gave you hope for the future of the scene. Two years and a great deal of touring later, do you still see a generational difference in how people approach Goth and Post-Punk, or has that picture become more complicated? Hugo: We are starting to notice more youngsters in the audience in Europe too. And that’s amazing. Precisely here in Stockholm we have a really nice and growing scene of young people making music, DJing, going to shows, and that’s great to see. Karo: A band with a long catalogue eventually develops an unwritten contract with its audience: there are sounds, songs and emotional qualities people expect. Do those expectations ever become creatively restrictive, or can they provide a useful resistance to work against? Alex: We’re always prepared to get caked by disappointed fans. We still get comments from people who miss a fourth member to fill the void of a second guitar. Thankfully, we’re in good company. The large majority of our followers are right there with us. Wherever we go, they follow. And wherever they point, we go. Karo: Then Comes Silence have always drawn from older Goth and Post-Punk traditions without sounding like a historical reconstruction. As that original musical history moves further into the past, what makes the difference between inheritance and nostalgia for you? Hugo: I think that we’re definitely not a nostalgia band. We don’t try to sound retro. But we listen to a lot of different genres, and most of the music we listen to is old. I mean, we are not trying to sound like Sisters of Mercy, The Mission or Lords of the New Church, but we probably have the same influences they had back then. Karo: The imagery surrounding “Requiem Ballroom” revolves around symbolic death, transformation and renewal. After more than a decade as a band, does the idea of renewal mean something different now than it would have when Then Comes Silence began in 2012? Alex: No, the only differences would be practical ones. A new instrument, new effects pedals, or a new producer behind the mix. The artistic renewal will always come from within. Karo: Looking beyond this album, what question about Then Comes Silence remains unresolved for you? What are you still trying to understand about this band that eight albums have not answered yet? Alex: Artistically, I have no comments and no expectations about what’s to come. I feel no anxiety about the music, and I don’t really care what other people say. But on the other hand, I’m trying to understand why we can’t make a living from what we do, and why it’s so difficult to reach a wider audience. The inflation affecting everyone on this planet doesn’t seem to apply to artists. People still don’t want to pay more for a show ticket, while they seem willing to pay twice as much for gas, milk or eggs in the store. Touring artists are facing higher and higher expenses, and many of them would probably need to cancel shows just to make ends meet. But they don’t, because there simply aren’t any realistic alternatives for live music. It must be even harder for the new young generation of musicians. I can’t see why it wouldn’t be. I’m trying to understand it, but I still haven’t found a good answer. About Then Comes Silence Then Comes Silence were formed in Stockholm in 2012 by vocalist, bassist and keyboard player Alex Svenson. Drummer Jonas Fransson joined in 2015, followed by guitarist Hugo Zombie in 2018; since 2022, the band have operated as a three-piece. Their discography has moved through labels including Novoton, Nuclear Blast, SPV and Metropolis Records, while extensive touring has taken them across Europe, North America and, in 2026, Latin America. Their eighth studio album, “Requiem Ballroom,” will be released on 20 November 2026 via Metropolis Records. Structured as two contrasting halves, Requiem and Ballroom, the album uses darkness and light not simply as visual motifs but as different approaches to arrangement and production. The current singles are “Judgement Day” and “Remaker Redeemer,” with the latter introducing the Ballroom side and its themes of rebirth, cleansing and beginning again.

items.body: It has been about four years since the Brazilian act Aesthetische released their last full-length album, but in the meantime, Gui Pires and Fab Viscardi have kept us entertained with an annual EP. “Every Beat Matters” serves as a metaphor for everything we can do to fight injustice, fascism, prejudice, war, and more. Musically, this translates into four brand-new tracks followed by three remixes. Aesthetische return to their roots more than ever, recalling their former project, Aghast View, with a sound deeply rooted in EBM. It is a meticulously crafted production boasting rich soundscapes and razor-sharp basslines that once again bring Front Line Assembly to mind. The tracks are driven by stomping beats that give them maximum club appeal. To my ears, the first three tracks all sound like potential singles, although Aesthetische clearly have a soft spot for “Chew The Loop,” which appears in three additional and strong remixes. The vocals round everything out, complemented by well-placed samples. One track remains instrumental, yet sounds incredibly effective. Aesthetische never disappoint, but this new EP is undoubtedly one of their strongest releases to date. It represents intelligent, impactful EBM. (Rating:9). Side-Line reported the release of “Every Beat Matters” on June 26, 2026 via Alfa Matrix. Listen to “Chew The Loop”’: Chew The Loop by Aesthetische About Aesthetische Aesthetische is a Brazilian EBM/industrial duo formed by Gui Pires and Fab Viscardi in 2012. Both musicians were previously known for their work in Aghast View and Biopsy, one of Brazil’s pioneering electro-industrial acts of the 1990s. After Aghast View, the duo launched Aesthetische as a new vehicle for modern EBM fused with trance, techno-body music, and industrial atmospheres. The band signed with Belgian label Alfa Matrix in 2012 and has since maintained an exclusive release partnership with them, issuing a steady discography of albums, EPs, and digital singles across physical and digital formats. Albums “Powerswitch” (2012, Alfa Matrix) – Issued in multiple editions, including a box version. “HybridCore” (2014, Alfa Matrix) – A follow-up blending hard-hitting EBM with more melodic synth textures. “Co3xist3ns3” (2019, Alfa Matrix) – Marked a return after several years, further exploring hybridized EBM and trance. “Rvprty” (2022, Alfa Matrix AM 3400DJ) – A digital-only release containing ten tracks. Singles & EPs “Nachtbrenner” (2013, Alfa Matrix) “Statement / Amplitude Zero” (2013, Alfa Matrix) “Colder Lights EP” (2014, Alfa Matrix) “Dirt And Basslines” (2015, Alfa Matrix) “Cold Is Clean” (2015, Alfa Matrix) “We Follow Blindly” (2016, Alfa Matrix) “In My Aurora” (2017, Alfa Matrix) – Featuring Noemi Aurora on vocals. “MMXX” (2020, Alfa Matrix) “Overflow” (2021, Alfa Matrix) “Boiling Over EP” (2023, Alfa Matrix) “Confidence Is Silent” (2024, Alfa Matrix) Split EP “4.4U [2012.11]” (2012, Alfa Matrix) – Digital compilation shared with Metroland, Mentallo & The Fixer, and Daniel B. Prothèse. Alfa Matrix has continued the pace since, following “Boiling Over” (2023) with “Confidence Is Silent” (2024), “Selling Fear” (2025) and now “Every Beat Matters” in 2026.

items.body: 33 takes the traditional age of Christ at his death as the axis of a twelve-part electroacoustic cycle concerned with creation, incarnation, suffering, death and renewal. Yara Mekawei and Amir Rezk draw on biblical passages, Coptic Orthodox liturgy and Arabic recitation, but rarely allow the texts to remain intact: voices are repeated, stretched and submerged until scripture begins to function as rhythm and texture. Dense drones, fractured percussion, recitation and sudden clearings give the record a ceremonial character without turning it into devotional music. Its structure is particularly effective. “LOGOS” begins with John’s “In the beginning was the Word”; by “New Creation,” Revelation has replaced Genesis, with the first heaven and earth passing away and death itself disappearing. Between them, “Mysterion,” “33,” “Harrowing of Hades” and “Sackcloth Love” trace a passage through Eucharist, Crucifixion, descent and mourning. Musically, 33 sits between electroacoustic composition, dark ambient, and industrial electronics with a hint of prog rock, although none of those descriptions quite accounts for its restless construction. Mekawei and Rezk work with low drones, distorted orchestral sonorities, spoken voices, granular processing and percussion that repeatedly breaks apart just as it appears to settle into a pattern. The music can be oppressively dense, then abruptly hollowed out to expose a voice or a thin electronic residue. Rather than using electronics as accompaniment to the religious texts, the pair subject voice and instrumental material to the same processes: syllables become pulses, recitation turns into noise, and acoustic sounds lose their identifiable origins. This constant movement between intelligibility and abstraction gives the album much of its tension. What begins with a private anxiety surrounding the age of 33 expands into a work about mortality and transformation, with ancient texts treated not as historical artefacts but as material that can still be sounded, fractured and inhabited. To help us further navigate the album, we reached out directly to Yara Mekawei and Amir Rezk. 33 seems to follow an unusually coherent spiritual trajectory: from the Logos and creation in “LOGOS” and “Genesis,” through embodiment, suffering and death, to resurrection and finally the New Jerusalem in “New Creation.” Yet the album never feels like a straightforward retelling of scripture; texts are fragmented, repeated, obscured and absorbed into the electronics. Did you conceive the twelve tracks as a narrative or liturgical cycle from the outset, and how important was it that this progression could be felt without necessarily being understood literally? From the very beginning, we did not set out to create a straightforward textual retelling or a literal recitation of scripture. For us, the sacred texts are not static history; they are a living, sonic score. The progression across the twelve tracks was essential because we recognized that the trajectory of Christ’s life, from incarnation and embodiment, through suffering, descent, and ultimate renewal, is not merely a historical or theological timeline. It is a universal, spiritual archetype. It is a pattern that exists in the world and plays out in our own lives, in human endurance, migration, grief, and rebirth, whether we consciously recognize it or not. By weaving Yara’s personal story, her family inheritance, her grandmother’s warning, her lived experience of displacement and transformation, into this grander framework, the album becomes a dual narrative. The fragmentation, repetition, and electronic processing of the texts reflect how personal memory and sacred history actually operate in human consciousness: rarely as a clean, linear text, but as lingering textures, echoes, and internal pictures. It was crucial that a listener could feel this emotional and spiritual weight instinctively without needing to decipher every word literally, because the underlying trajectory of endurance and transformation is something universally felt in the human spirit. The number 33 begins from something intensely personal — a maternal warning about the thirty-third year of life — but the album gradually connects that age to Christ’s suffering, death and resurrection. In the title track especially, the language of Isaiah’s suffering servant and the Crucifixion seems to make personal vulnerability and sacred history overlap. How did that private association with the age of 33 become the organising principle of the record, and did making the album change what that number meant to you? The connection became obvious the moment we realized that 33 was not just a personal chronological marker, but the darkest point in Christ’s earthly life, the threshold of Gethsemane and the Cross, where He faced an unrepeatable cup of unknown suffering and abandonment. In our own human lives, those rock-bottom moments, where we carry an unbearable personal weight or face severe displacement, often become the precise pivots for profound transformation. The warning Yara inherited about the thirty-third year was essentially pointing toward this exact kind of personal Gethsemane: a room where you are tested to your limits, forcing a parallel between our lived vulnerability and what Christ endured. Creating 33 completely changed what that number means to us. Through the process of writing and immersing ourselves in these detailed sonic patterns and raw emotions, 33 transformed from an ominous, looming warning into a symbol of profound solidarity. It fixed a truth in our minds: our suffering in this life is never meaningless, nor is it carried in isolation. The Divine chose to step into human history and share directly in our exact grief, exile, and pain. Through making this record, the thirty-third year ceased to be a room of fear, becoming instead a reminder that we are never truly alone in the dark. Sacred language in 33 occupies a strange position between meaning and sound. Biblical passages, Coptic Orthodox material, Arabic and other vocal fragments can initially be intelligible, but repetition and electronic processing often push them toward rhythm, texture or something resembling incantation. Yara, your previous work has already explored ways of translating sacred texts into sonic structures; how did the two of you approach the voice here? Were you interested in preserving the theological meaning of these texts, or in reaching a point where the sound of devotion itself becomes the compositional material? For us, it was never a choice between preserving theological meaning or turning the text into pure abstraction, we wanted both. We approached the sacred texts as both a coherent narrative framework and a stream of subconscious thought, treating the voice as a primary musical texture. We deeply respect the inherent power of music to imprint a specific fingerprint upon the mind and the soul. However, we wouldn’t use the word “incantation” to describe this process. Instead, we see the voice and its electronic transformations as a sonic blessing carried through the physical sound waves themselves. We knew that many people listening across the world wouldn’t understand Arabic or Coptic, but we believed that sound itself can transcend language barriers. By layering, repeating, and processing these sacred fragments, we wanted to carry the spiritual energy and raw devotion directly to the listener’s intuition. The theological meaning grounds the structure, while the sonic vibration allows the blessing to reach anyone who listens, regardless of whether they can translate the words. There is a striking circularity between the beginning and end of the album. “LOGOS” opens with John’s “In the beginning was the Word,” while “New Creation” ultimately arrives at Revelation’s vision of the first heaven and earth passing away, God wiping away every tear, and death ceasing to exist. Between those points, the music moves through creation, the body, Eucharist, suffering, mourning and resurrection. Do you think of 33 as moving from one creation to another — and, if so, is “new creation” primarily a Christian theological idea for you, or does it also describe a personal process of destruction and transformation that took place while making the record? It is deeply both: a personal process of transformation and a theological truth made manifest. On a personal and artistic level, 33 is our very first collaboration together, so the album itself is literally a “new creation” born from our two individual musical worlds. We share the belief that marrying the arts with the sacred is like bringing heaven and earth together, much like the Incarnation of the Divine Logos coming down to breathe new life into His creation and bloom into a new Tree of Life. J.R.R. Tolkien spoke of artists as “sub-creators” or co-creators alongside the Great Creator. By deliberately inviting the Divine into our sound, making a “new creation” was never about trying to invent a new genre of music; it was about marrying the eternal with the earthly, which makes the work spiritual and new at its core. Making this album was an essential process of bringing light directly into the desolation of our own personal suffering and “stations” of life. It was a way to ground those difficult experiences in hope and meaning, not just for ourselves, but hopefully for anyone who listens to the record. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: The Getaway could easily have stood on its own, but the remix sequence expands its central idea: fractured industrial sound behaving almost like an alien transmission, constantly mutating through minute edits, glitches, and rhythmic interference. Chiseled from front to back with remarkable precision The Getaway by Unterm Rad   Mike Slansky, operating as Unterm Rad, continues his run of punishing industrial IDM with The Getaway for the ever-consistent Bulgaria-based Mahorka imprint. With a background spanning audio engineering, expansive sound design, and graphic work reaching back to the Tympanik Audio era, Slansky was also a key component of the now-shuttered Point Source Electronic Arts collective. His work has long occupied darker electronic spaces, and The Getaway pushes further into that territory through an unusually constrained process: the album was composed entirely from short instrument clips and sounds supplied through Point Source’s Genome sample kits, each fragment carefully edited, processed, and sequenced until it evolved into something entirely new. No synthesizers, AI, or outside sound sources were used, adhering to the open-source spirit of the Genome project. Seven original pieces emerge as dark-grey slabs of machinery, where microscopic edits and fractured rhythms give each track a strangely extraterrestrial charge. Up front, “Hang Me Out To Dry” drives through minimal industrial fissures with a beat-heavy barrage of rugged technoid tones, metallic grit, and tightly controlled distortion. “They’re On To Us” narrows the focus further, exposing Slansky’s precision-built rhythmic glitches as tiny mechanical movements seem to twitch beneath the surface, while “Cornered” opens into broken beats and cavernous echoes, giving the record a sense of mechanical engineer​ing operating somewhere far beyond human reach. Transparent details become increasingly exposed :: The final six pieces hand Slansky’s material over to Access to Arasaka, Evaluation Copy, Vaag, Feederwire, Hexalyne, and Cole, each pulling the source tracks into a distinct interpretation. Rather than simply extending the album, these remixes reveal just how much microscopic movement exists inside Slansky’s sound structures. Access to Arasaka and Hexalyne sharpen the material into brisk, erratic sci-fi electro-nics; Evaluation Copy scorches through beats and bass; Vaag bends the rhythms into flexible broken beat contortions; and Feederwire drags everything through piercing industrial low-end vibrations. Cole’s closing interpretation is perhaps the most surreal, stripping the machinery back until its strange, transparent details become increasingly exposed. The Getaway could easily have stood on its own, but the remix sequence expands its central idea: fractured industrial sound behaving almost like an alien transmission, constantly mutating through minute edits, glitches, and rhythmic interference. Closing with “The Walls Are Closing In,” before the remixes kick in, Slansky lets pressure evaporate into sparse technoid shifts, leaving behind an album that feels both rigorously engineered and strangely alive. By opening his source material to collaborators, he turns a tightly controlled sonic experiment into a broader study of industrial texture, glitch mechanics, and extraterrestrial electronics—chiseled from front to back with remarkable precision. The Getaway is available on Mahorka. [Bandcamp] The Getaway by Unterm RadThe post Unterm Rad :: The Getaway (Mahorka) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Review by brainsuccasurgery — The Science of the Seasons in 4 Points. Before discussing *La Scienza delle Stagioni*, Andrea Orlando's second album, it might be helpful to review the following preliminary points:1. The Bands. Andrea Orlando is the drummer on all four albums by La Coscienza Di Cena, an RPI band founded in Genoa in 2007, which released a superb self-titled debut album in 2011 and three other highly recommended albums between 2013 and 2018. Is it worth noting here that Genoa (Genova) is the birthplace of the illustrious PFM, one of the founding fathers of Italian progressive rock (RPI)?Before the formation of La Coscienza Di Cena, Andrea Orlando had already gained some recognition in this microcosm as a member of what it's fair to call the "Zuffanti nebula"?a transalpine prog music collective that began to coalesce around the Genoese bassist Fabio Zuffanti in the early '90s and gained greater visibility with Finisterre's debut album (1995).2. The Artist. Andrea Orlando joined Finisterre as early as 1997 on their *Live at Progday* and then on the fabulous *In Ogni Luogo* (1999), before returning for the 2019 comeback album. Orlando also played drums on *Mirrogames* (1998) by H�stsonaten, Zuffanti's other major band. In both cases, Orlando replaced Marco Cavani. To round out this overview, it's worth noting that drummer Andrea Orlando also contributed to the album by La Curva di Lesmo (2015), a duo that Zuffanti formed with Stefano Agnini, one of the two keyboardists on La Coscienza. And that brings us partially full circle.Let's now turn to the album itself by going over the other two points:3. The musicians. Since Andrea Orlando is one of the stalwarts of this famous Genoese music scene, it's no surprise that for his two solo albums, he called on other members of that same scene. For example, to give credit where credit is due, Zuffanti himself plays bass on one track from *La Scienza delle Stagioni*, and Boris Valle (Finisterre's longtime keyboardist) plays piano on another. Orlando, an accomplished drummer but also a capable keyboardist (with a predilection for the mellotron and organ), here cedes the piano parts?in addition to Valle?to Luca Scherani (H�stsonaten, La Coscienza di Zeno, La Curva di Lesmo) and to Agostino Marco (Finisterre, La Maschera, Zaal) for the Moog solos.On *Dalla Vita Autentica*, Andrea Orlando's previous solo album, the majority of the electric guitar parts were performed by two highly talented musicians: Marcella Arganese?who can be found in Ubi Maior and who regularly dazzles us with *Samura� of Prog*?and Laura Marsano, whom we've seen on Zuffanti's solo albums and those of drummer Maurizio Di Tollo. Two women on guitar?and not just any women?is rare enough to be worth noting, whatever the critics of "wokism" may say. On *La Scienza delle Stagioni*, Marcella has been replaced by Stefano Marelli, but Laura Marsano is always there to treat us to her poignant solos (the slow "Stagione Lontana"). The young singer Meghi Moschino contributes her calm, medium-toned voice to five of the seven tracks?a voice that reminds me a bit of Laura Mombrini's (Prowlers). On *Dalla Vita Autentica*, the robust vocals of Alessandro Corvaglia (another essential, ubiquitous figure on the RPI scene for several years), paired with those of Simona Angioloni (remember *Aries*, the band formed in the 2000s with? Zuffanti, him again), gave the whole a more robust feel. A matter of taste.4. The music. *La Scienza delle Stagioni* alternates between dynamic, vibrant tracks rooted in PFM's sun-drenched RPI, and tenderly romantic moments that unfold into expansive, emotionally charged symphonic prog, closer in style to *Hostsonaten*. By elegantly blending these two styles, the diptych "Il Sogno di Anastasia" (12:12) stands out as one of the album's most compelling tracks. In addition to "Il Sogno di Anastasia ? Parte Seconda," a lovely musical reverie with enchanting undertones, the album includes another instrumental, "City 40" (6:36), a sort of high-energy Latin version of "Samurai of Prog."The influence of Camel, noticeable from the very start of the previous album ("Le Forme Della Distanza"), is less pronounced throughout *La Scienza delle Stagioni*, giving way to more personal ideas, resulting in a kind of symphonic neo-prog with strong RPI influences. On the other hand, the extensive and frequent use of the mellotron (the long intro to "Stagione Lontana" with its celestial tones, or that of "La Strada del Ritorno," among others) draws the most serene moments toward the most ethereal Scandinavian prog.Of roughly similar length, the epic closing track, the highly symphonic "La Strada del Ritorno" (15:01), can be compared to the thrilling "Dalla Vita Autentica" (16:52), which closed the 2017 album of the same name, illuminated by an unforgettable solo by Marcella Arganese. But despite some structural and musical similarities, the comparison ultimately favors the latter, which is more ambitious and features more inspired melodies. Yet the melancholy that envelops the final section of "La Strada del Ritorno"?enhanced by Meghi's angelic voice and the serene appearance of the English and French horns?ultimately moves us, giving us the impression that a pale winter sun has come to breathe its loving breath upon us.At first glance, *La Scienza delle Stagioni* seems a little less striking than its predecessor, *Dalla Vita Autentica*. At the very least, it builds on its predecessor's strengths while retaining all its qualities, though without reaching quite the same heights. But let's not be fooled by first impressions. There are prog albums that possess a kind of natural clarity, made up of music whose beauty is immediately apparent; and others, like *La Scienza delle Stagioni*, that save their magic for a little later, revealing it just after we've finished listening, when we think we've moved on to something else. But that is the secret art of these mysterious works: to prepare for us an immediate future more beautiful than expected. *La Scienza delle Stagioni* possesses that special magic that fairies bestow as they lean over the cradle of certain works?a magic that stays with you and illuminates your path long after the notes have faded away.

items.body: Review by greenpete — They made a startlingly confident beginning with their exuberant, minor-label debut, An Evening With Dando Shaft (no, not a live album). But Dando Shaft's high-water mark arrived with this, their sophomore LP (often called the "Carousel" album, and released on RCA's short-lived Neon label, which only issued 11 albums total). This record dispenses entirely with drums, plunging deeper into varied, lyrical progressive folk. Singer Polly Bolton, from the wonderfully named village of Leamington Spa, joined the boys to bolster their string intricacies with her breathy, Sandy Denny-esque voice. The debut was marred only by the awkward "The Cat Song," but on the Carousel album, there's really not a bad cut. The Bulgarian-rhythmic songs of dual guitarists Dave Cooper and Kevin Dempsey, and mega-instrumentalist Martin Jenkins, are consistently strong, with Jenkins' mandolin, flute, and fiddle shining here. His tune "Whispering Ned," about a gent who enjoys indulging in sugar cubes (and whom the band evidently knew) adds an imaginative twist to the canon of drug songs. The upbeat "Pass it On" is notable for its exuberant chorus about values that have, sadly, since gone out of style. But the real highlights are "Till the Morning Comes" and "River Boat." Both feature Bolton's angelic vocals, the former a wispy duet with Cooper graced by luscious, gently psychedelic flute (Jenkins) and tablas (Ted Kay); and the latter an utterly breathtaking, pastoral delight that conjures green, rural England in poem-song.Bolton would stick around for Lantaloon, a good but inessential album, then depart after tiring of feeling like a "guest" vocalist. So if you plan to only get one album by this highly underappreciated psych-folk band...take a ride on the Carousel.- greenpete
