items.body: Mesh will release the mini-album “Fallen Angel” on Dependent Records on 27 November 2026. The British duo of Mark Hockings and Richard Silverthorn describe the nine-track record as an addendum to this year’s album “The Truth Doesn’t Matter” rather than the start of a new chapter, built from songs that grew out of writing sessions the pair started after touring behind that record. The label had asked for a fourth single from “The Truth Doesn’t Matter”; Hockings and Silverthorn instead wrote enough new material for close to half an album of additional songs. “Fallen Angel” combines four newly written tracks with remixes and a live recording, offering what the band calls a deeper dive into the themes of “The Truth Doesn’t Matter”. Pre-orders for “Fallen Angel” open on 24 September, the same day the mini-album’s fourth single from that campaign, “Trying to Save You”, arrives on streaming platforms in a mix by Olaf Wollschläger. The title track follows as a single on 21 October with a new music video featuring the band, ahead of the full CD and vinyl release on 27 November. The tracklist: Fallen Angel Protect Your Neck Not This Time The Meeting of the Broken Tilt Trying to Save You (single mix) The Truth Doesn’t Matter (live, recorded on this tour) Fallen Angel (extended version) Trying to Save You (remix) “Fallen Angel”, “Protect Your Neck”, “Not This Time” and “The Meeting of the Broken” are entirely new songs; “Tilt” receives its first physical release. Mark Hockings and Richard Silverthorn wrote and recorded all tracks and produced the mini-album with Vaughn George on live keyboards and Sean Suleman on live drums; it was recorded at Mesh HQ and The Summerhouse in Bristol, mixed by Olaf Wollschläger and Mesh at Cottonbeat Studio in Burscheid, Germany, with additional mastering by Wollschläger. Mark Hockings supplied the artwork and photography, with additional artwork, editing and layout by Nico Janse van Rensburg. “Fallen Angel” will be released as a jewel case CD, a limited clear vinyl LP capped at 500 copies, and a standard black vinyl LP; the CD and a KitAlbum Tour Edition will be available at Mesh’s live shows roughly six weeks ahead of the wider release. Distribution runs through SPKR. At least two of the new songs will be played live starting with Mesh’s show in Krefeld, Germany, on 1 October. The band’s confirmed live dates through November: 1 October 2026 – Krefeld, Germany – Kulturfabrik 2 October 2026 – Braunschweig, Germany – Westand 3 October 2026 – Dresden, Germany – Reithalle Strasse E 4 October 2026 – Berlin, Germany – Kesselhaus 5 November 2026 – Łódź, Poland – Klub Scenografia 6 November 2026 – Halle/Saale, Germany – Capitol 7 November 2026 – Liberec, Czech Republic – Dům Kultury Liberec (Sever Synth Festival) Hockings and Silverthorn also confirmed that “Looking Skyward” is set to return on red vinyl “very, very soon”, and that “Who Watches Over Me?” will receive a 25th-anniversary reissue in 2027 as an art book edition with refreshed artwork, following the return of its rights from Sony Music; that album will also return to streaming platforms next year. The details emerged during a Zoom Q&A with Hockings and Silverthorn on 22 September, which Mesh had previously teased as previewing an “unusual release”. About Mesh Mesh formed in 1991 in the UK when vocalist and guitarist Mark Hockings and keyboard player and vocalist Richard Silverthorn began writing together, later joined by keyboardist Neil Taylor. The band released the “Fragile” EP in 1994 and its debut album, “In This Place Forever”, in 1996, followed by “The Point at Which It Falls Apart” in 1999, reissued in a 25th-anniversary edition in 2024. The major-label release “Who Watches Over Me?” in 2002 widened the band’s European audience, especially in Germany, and 2006’s “We Collide” was produced with former Depeche Mode collaborator Gareth Jones. “Automation Baby” (2013) reached number 33 on the German album chart, and “Looking Skyward” (2016) climbed to number 12 there. Mesh continued as the core duo of Hockings and Silverthorn, touring with drummer Sean Suleman and additional live keyboard players, and added Vaughn George to the live lineup in April 2023. Hockings also records solo as Blackcarburning, releasing the album “Watching Sleepers” and the EP “Divide Us”. Mesh’s most recent album, “The Truth Doesn’t Matter”, arrived in 2026 on Dependent Records, preceded by the singles “Exile”, “Hey Stranger” and “This World” and followed by a European tour; “Fallen Angel”, out 27 November 2026, extends that album cycle with new songs, remixes and a live recording.

items.body: Conscience, the German electropop and synthpop project of Rüdiger Illg, releases the compilation “Uncharted Vol. 1 (The Singles 2009-2023)” on Echozone on 25 September 2026. It gathers Conscience’s single releases from that period into one set, adds one new song and three new mixes, and presents every track remastered. The label describes a second volume, “Uncharted Vol. 2”, as already in the works. Despite the plural billing Echozone sometimes gives the project, Conscience remains a one-man operation: Illg writes, plays and produces every track himself at Science2, his home studio in Leeste, Lower Saxony. He formed Conscience in 1991, but “Uncharted Vol. 1” starts its clock at 2009, not at the project’s founding. Echozone explains why: Conscience did not sign a record deal until 1998, with the “Hardware” EP, and that contract proved short-lived. Illg then signed to Echozone, whose own account of the compilation dates that move to around 2008, when “Theatre Of Deception” served as the lead single for the album “Gravity Has Gone”; Side-Line’s earlier research into the project’s Echozone catalogue had put that signing a year later, in 2009. Physical releases stopped soon after over cost, and for years Conscience issued albums and EPs with no accompanying singles at all. That changed with the 2020 album “Sentient”, after which every Conscience album has carried multiple single releases, the run “Uncharted Vol. 1” now compiles. The compilation follows the single “Explain Everything”, which Echozone issued on 28 August 2026 as an advance taste of the same collection. About Conscience Rüdiger Illg founded Conscience in August 1991, working first with a single Yamaha SY22 synthesizer, and has written, played and produced every track since under that name at Science2. He also records as Science O.C.N. and Chaos Network. The project’s first six years produced cassette-only releases traded through the tape network, followed by a first CD in 1998 and a run of CD-Rs through the early 2000s. NewEx Records picked up Conscience in 2007, and Illg signed to Echozone in 2009, a relationship that has produced the bulk of the catalogue since, including the albums “Phases³” (2025) and “Suspended In Time” (2026) and the singles and EPs “Uncharted Vol. 1” now draws its selections from. Guest vocalists across the catalogue have included Colin Angus of The Shamen and Dan Söderqvist of Twice a Man. “Uncharted Vol. 1 (The Singles 2009-2023)” is Conscience’s first compilation to collect that stretch of the catalogue in one release, with a second volume already planned.

items.body: Front Line Assembly released their eighth studio album, “Hard Wired,” through Off Beat on 25 September 1995, with Metropolis Records handling North America and Energy Rekords issuing the record in Sweden. It was the Canadian electro-industrial band’s first release for the German label. The album turns 31 this year. Bill Leeb and Rhys Fulber produced the record and wrote all ten tracks, which run 62 minutes: “Neologic Spasm,” “Paralyzed,” “Re-Birth,” “Circuitry,” “Mortal” (instrumental), “Modus Operandi,” “Transparent Species,” “Barcode,” “Condemned” and “Infra Red Combat.” Greg Reely engineered and mixed, with Delwyn Brooks assisting, continuing a working partnership that began on “Caustic Grip” in 1990. Devin Townsend played electric guitar, returning after his session work on the previous year’s “Millennium.” Dave McKean produced the illustration, design and photography. The sessions ran roughly five months at the Warehouse. Leeb wrote the lyrics only once the music was finished, and described that order as the band’s normal method rather than a choice made for this record: “We write […] the music and then once we’ve got it finished, then I sit at home and start on the lyrics. I can’t imagine writing any other way. […] I think with our music it’s usually the sounds that inspire us.” On what those lyrics deal with, he set materialism and environmental collapse against the technology driving both: “I think most of the lyrics are basically about man versus technology. Basically, we’re destroying our planet with technology. At the same time, technology is the only thing that can save us. It’s this constant struggle between these two forces that is making us go in whatever direction we’re all going.” That reading runs through the sampling as well. The album draws audio from “True Romance,” “In the Mouth of Madness,” “Lifeforce,” “Stargate,” “Speed,” “The Puppet Masters,” “No Escape,” “Romeo Is Bleeding,” “The Crow,” “Lethal Weapon” and “Alien 3,” alongside sound effects from the 1993 video game “Doom” and passages from three Aphex Twin recordings. “Circuitry” was the album’s only single, released on 31 October 1995. Its limited edition came as a two-CD digipak with remixes by Haujobb and Biosphere, a mixed-mode first disc carrying the “Millennium” video and photo galleries, and a second disc with the non-album tracks “Destructive Transformation” and “Hydrogen.” The album reached number 47 on the Swedish albums chart and the single number 32 on the Swedish singles chart. “Hard Wired” has sold at least 50,000 copies worldwide, and its 5,000-copy limited edition sold out in two weeks. A further track from the same sessions, “Plasticity,” was held back and issued separately; Fulber explained the decision in commercial terms: “We kept it off the album to release later […] It gives people a reason to check it out because if you release it as a single that is already on album no one is really going to care.” The “Plasticity” video won Best Alternative Video at the MuchMusic Video Awards in Toronto in 1996. The album has returned to shelves twice since. Black Rain Records pressed a 500-copy picture vinyl in August 2011, cut to seven songs, dropping “Mortal,” “Modus Operandi” and “Transparent Species.” For the record’s twentieth year, Artoffact Records issued a 300-copy vinyl box in 2015 pairing the album with the “Live Wired” live record and the “Circuitry” single, all remastered by Reely; Side-Line reported that The Front Line Assembly 6LP boxset ‘Hard Wired’ is almost sold out that May, and covered the same year’s news that Front Line Assembly finally see ‘Plasticity’ released on a 10 inch vinyl (3 formats). “Hard Wired” streams on Spotify. About Front Line Assembly Bill Leeb formed Front Line Assembly in Vancouver, Canada, in 1986, shortly after leaving Skinny Puppy, where he had contributed bass synth and backing vocals between 1985 and 1986 under the name Wilhelm Schroeder. He picked the band name to reflect his view that strength lies in working together. The demo tapes “Nerve War” and “Total Terror” were limited to 100 copies each and mostly passed around among friends, with Rhys Fulber contributing as an unofficial member. The project’s first appearance on record was “Aggression,” on the 1987 Third Mind compilation “For Your Ears Only.” Belgian label KK issued the debut album “The Initial Command” at the end of 1987, with Fulber and Michael Balch assisting, and German label Dossier released “State of Mind” in January 1988. When a planned Nettwerk release fell through, Third Mind put out “Corrosion” and the “Disorder” EP later that year, then signed the band to a three-album deal and licensed “Corrosion” to Wax Trax! for North America. Balch became an official member in 1988 and left after the 1989 “Gashed Senses & Crossfire” tour to join Ministry and Revolting Cocks. Fulber replaced him and appeared on “Caustic Grip” (1990), the album that started the band’s long partnership with engineer Greg Reely and introduced guitar on “Provision” and “Resist.” Chris Peterson debuted as live percussionist on the tour that followed in early 1991. “Tactical Neural Implant” (1992) turned toward more melodic, multi-layered arrangements and the heavy film sampling that became a fixture of the sound. Five remixes for Fear Factory’s “Fear Is the Mindkiller” EP in 1993 fed directly into “Millennium” (1994), the band’s first industrial metal record, built on metal guitar samples and Devin Townsend’s session work. “Hard Wired” arrived the following September. Fulber left in 1997 to concentrate on production, and Peterson took his place for “FLAvour of the Weak” (1997), “Implode” (1999) and “Epitaph” (2001), a run that traded the metal influences for breakbeat and big beat. Fulber returned for “Civilization” (2004), and Peterson rejoined for “Artificial Soldier” (2006), the first album to feature Jeremy Inkel and Jared Slingerland. “Improvised Electronic Device” (2010), “Echogenetic” (2013), “Wake Up the Coma” (2019) and “Mechanical Soul” (2021) followed, the last on Metropolis. The band also composed soundtracks for the games “Quake III: Team Arena,” “AirMech” and “WarMech.” Inkel died on 23 January 2018 at the age of 34, from complications of an asthma condition. Leeb has run Delerium since 1987 and Noise Unit since the late 1980s, while Fulber started Conjure One after his 1997 departure and has worked with Fear Factory for decades; Side-Line published a Front Line Assembly interview – Catching up with Bill Leeb and Rhys Fulber in 2024. “Hard Wired” turns 31 this year, the record that closed out the guitar-driven stretch the band opened with “Millennium” before the electronics took over again.

items.body: Gang of Four, the English post-punk band from Leeds, released their debut album “Entertainment!” on 25 September 1979 through EMI, with Warner Bros. Records handling North America. The album turns 47 this year. It runs 39 minutes and 53 seconds across twelve tracks and was recorded that same year at The Workhouse on the Old Kent Road in London. Jon King and Andy Gill produced it with the band’s then-manager Rob Warr, and Rik Walton engineered. The line-up was King on lead vocals, percussion and melodica, Gill on electric guitar and vocals, Dave Allen on bass and Hugo Burnham on drums. EMI had signed the group after its debut release, the three-track “Damaged Goods” EP, issued on 13 October 1978 by Bob Last’s Edinburgh label Fast Product and recorded at Cargo Studios in Rochdale. Two of those three tracks, “Damaged Goods” and “Love Like Anthrax”, were re-recorded for the album. The running order is “Ether”, “Natural’s Not in It”, “Not Great Men”, “Damaged Goods”, “Return the Gift”, “Guns Before Butter”, “I Found That Essence Rare”, “Glass”, “Contract”, “At Home He’s a Tourist”, “5.45” and “Love Like Anthrax”. King wrote the lyrics under the influence of Situationism, the writing of Michel Foucault and Jacques Lacan, feminism and Marx’s theory of alienation. He also designed the sleeve, which reproduces a still from a Winnetou film in three processed versions, with a text reading: “The Indian smiles, he thinks that the cowboy is his friend. The cowboy smiles, he is glad the Indian is fooled. Now he can exploit him.” “At Home He’s a Tourist” reached number 58 in the UK Singles Chart, still the highest placing of any Gang of Four song. The band were booked to perform it on Top of the Pops, but the producers asked them to change the line “and the rubbers you hide in your top left pocket” to “rubbish”; the group refused and the appearance was cancelled. The album peaked at number 45 on the UK Albums Chart and number 35 in New Zealand. Writing in Rolling Stone in August 1980, David Fricke called it “the best debut album by a British band – punk or otherwise – since the original English release of The Clash”. About Gang of Four Gang of Four formed in Leeds in 1976 around guitarist Andy Gill and singer Jon King, who had met as students. Drummer Hugo Burnham and bassist Dave Wolfson completed the first line-up; after two or three gigs Wolfson was replaced by Dave Allen in 1977. Fast Product released the “Damaged Goods” EP in October 1978, and EMI signed the band the following year. “Entertainment!” arrived in September 1979 and was followed by “Solid Gold” in March 1981 and “Songs of the Free” in 1982, the latter carrying “I Love a Man in Uniform”, which was dropped from BBC playlists during the Falklands conflict. Allen left in 1981 after two albums and went on to co-found Shriekback; Busta “Cherry” Jones filled in before Sara Lee joined as the permanent bassist. Burnham left in 1982 and Steve Goulding took over the drum stool for “Hard” (1983). The band split in 1984. Gill and King reconvened three times in the 1990s, recording “Mall” (1991) with Gail Ann Dorsey on bass and “Shrinkwrapped” (1995). The founding four reunited in 2004 and toured the UK in 2005, releasing the re-recorded “Return the Gift” on 28 September 2005 and performing “Entertainment!” in full for the All Tomorrow’s Parties Don’t Look Back series that year; Side-Line covered the band’s later live material in Exclusive preview Gang Of Four’s ‘Live…In The Moment’ live album. Burnham departed again in late 2005 to return to teaching, and Allen was replaced by Thomas McNeice in 2008. King left in 2011 after disagreements with Gill, and John Sterry took over vocals. That line-up issued “Content” (2011), “What Happens Next” (2015) and “Happy Now” (2019). Andy Gill died on 1 February 2020, aged 64, ending that incarnation of the band. In October 2021 King reformed Gang of Four with Burnham, Sara Lee and Slint guitarist David Pajo for a tour of 1977 to 1983 material. Lee was replaced by Linda Pardee in January 2024 and then by Gail Greenwood that July, and Pajo by Ted Leo in January 2025. Dave Allen died in April 2025, aged 69, having lived with early-onset dementia. The band played its final show in Amsterdam on 6 July 2025. The record’s reach outlasted the band. Die Krupps recorded a version of “To Hell With Poverty” for their 2021 covers album, as reported in Die Krupps cover Gang Of Four with new single ‘To Hell With Poverty’. Michael Stipe has said of the band: “Gang of Four could really swing. I stole a lot from them.” Rolling Stone placed “Entertainment!” at number 490 on its 500 Greatest Albums list in 2003, number 483 in 2012 and number 273 in 2020, and Kevin J. H. Dettmar wrote a book on it for the 33 1/3 series in 2014. Forty-seven years on, the debut remains the album on which the Leeds four-piece set its guitar, bass and drums against lyrics about commodities, contracts and the news.

items.body: Rammstein‘s “Herzeleid” turns 31 this year. Motor Music released the debut studio album by the Berlin Neue Deutsche Härte and industrial metal band on 25 September 1995. Producer Jacob Hellner oversaw the sessions at Polar Studios and his own BomKrash studio in Stockholm, Sweden, with Dutch engineer Ronald Prent mixing. “Herzeleid” runs eleven tracks and 49:22, all written by the band. The tracklist comprises “Wollt ihr das Bett in Flammen sehen”, “Der Meister”, “Weißes Fleisch”, “Asche zu Asche”, “Seemann”, “Du riechst so gut”, “Das alte Leid”, “Heirate mich”, “Herzeleid”, “Laichzeit” and “Rammstein”. Till Lindemann sang lead, with Richard Kruspe and Paul Landers on guitars, Oliver Riedel on bass, Christoph Schneider on drums and Christian “Flake” Lorenz on keyboards. “Du riechst so gut” preceded the album as its first single on 28 August 1995, followed by “Seemann” on 8 January 1996. The album initially sold slowly but climbed to No. 2 on the German Albums Chart on the strength of the band’s touring, and was later certified 2× Platinum in Germany. A remastered anniversary edition followed on 4 December 2020, released both digitally and on double heavyweight colored vinyl. About Rammstein Rammstein formed in Berlin in 1994. Guitarist Richard Kruspe, who had relocated from East to West Berlin in 1989 and played in the band Orgasm Death Gimmick, began working with bassist Oliver Riedel and drummer Christoph Schneider in 1993. Kruspe recruited vocalist Till Lindemann, then a basket weaver and drummer in the band First Arsch, after overhearing him sing. The group entered and won a 1994 Berlin contest for amateur bands, receiving a week of professional studio time; their winning demo drew guitarist Paul Landers into the project, and Landers in turn brought in keyboardist Christian “Flake” Lorenz from Feeling B, completing the six-piece lineup that has remained unchanged since. The band signed to Motor Music and began recording its debut album, “Herzeleid”, in March 1995 with producer Jacob Hellner, who would go on to produce five more Rammstein albums through 2009. “Du riechst so gut” appeared as the lead single that August, and “Herzeleid” followed on 25 September 1995. Rammstein spent the rest of 1995 opening for Project Pitchfork and Clawfinger before headlining their own German tour that December, building the live following that carried the album to eventual gold and platinum status. The band’s second album, “Sehnsucht” (1997), debuted at No. 1 in Germany and produced the singles “Engel” and “Du hast”, followed by the live album “Live aus Berlin” (1999). Rammstein signed with Universal Music and released “Mutter” in 2001, then “Reise, Reise” (2004) and “Rosenrot” (2005), each reaching the top of album charts across Europe. “Liebe ist für alle da” (2009) gave the band its first German No. 1 single with “Pussy”. After a recording hiatus spent touring, Rammstein released an untitled seventh album in 2019, which reached No. 1 in fourteen countries, followed by “Zeit” in 2022. On the 25th anniversary of “Herzeleid” in September 2020, the band announced the remastered anniversary edition of the album, released that December. “Herzeleid” remains Rammstein’s debut record and, thirty-one years on, the release that introduced the band’s sound and lineup essentially unchanged to today.

items.body: Mondträume is finally back in action with their first new album in seven years. The Spanish band remains driven by Pikotto VondMond, now officially joined by vocalist Nicky Schulschenk (known from N-Frequency). Schulschenk took over from Damasius Venys three years ago and has already featured on the band’s recent EPs. This new album delivers 12 tracks, while the ‘Deluxe Edition’ includes a bonus disc with another 12 songs, comprising additional tracks, remixes, and collaborations. Musically, Mondträume stays true to their infectious, danceable Future-Pop-driven sound. But can we still call it Future-Pop today? Is the genre due for a revival, or is this a kind of ‘Post-Future-Pop’ sound? Ultimately, it doesn’t really matter; the band simply does its own thing, resulting in a polished and complete-sounding album. Danceable rhythms underpin melodies that, devoid of excessive melancholy, come across as cheerful and uplifting. While there are occasional moody passages that provide some variation, the overall production is captivating. Here and there, you’ll notice subtle changes, such as harder, more EBM-oriented basslines, but this is simply part of the genre’s characteristic sound. Previously released tracks such as “Poisoned Love” and, especially, “Pictures Of You” remain fantastic songs that showcase Mondträume at their best. Replacing Damasius Venys was certainly a challenge, but there is clear chemistry between the new duo. Three tracks also feature female vocals by Madril. As mentioned earlier, the bonus disc offers 12 additional tracks, although these aren’t necessarily among my personal favorites. The remixes are the real highlights here, featuring contributions from established remixers such as Rob Dust, while Code 64 and Beyond Border also provide some pleasant surprises. There is even a sort of tribute to Bruderschaft in the form of a remix of “Falling” that Mondträume created some time ago. The ‘Deluxe Edition’ seems primarily aimed at the absolute die-hard fans, but the standard album will undoubtedly attract new listeners as well. Mondträume is back and continues to deliver high-quality Future-Pop. (Rating:8½). Side-Line reported the 2CD announcement for “Mindgames” back in April. The project released the “The Unknown Path” EP on Alfa Matrix in 2022, followed by the “Heart Machine” EP in 2023 and the “Poisoned Love” single in 2024, before “Mindgames”. Nicky Schulschenk, also known from N-Frequency, took over lead vocal duties from Damasius Venys and discussed the transition in a February 2025 Side-Line interview.

items.body: An obsession, exaggeration Lust, desire and adoration Lose yourself in someone else Limerence closes every door Robots In Love have the sort of name that promises chrome-plated heartbreak, and their latest single Cease and Desist delivers an emotional sucker punch. The New Zealand dark electronic duo of vocalist-producer Elenor Rayner and drummer-producer Alex Burchell builds the song around obsession gone feral: attraction narrowing into fixation, fixation hardening into dependency, and reason getting shoved somewhere beneath the furniture. There is no polite exit once the appetite starts feeding on itself. The guitars come down hard, with hardcore licks driven right up against industrial metal without quite falling into Ministry cosplay. There is some of SINE’s bruising electronic pressure here, along with the blackened mechanical weight of latter-day Gary Numan, while the bigger synth architecture brushes against HEALTH, Nine Inch Nails, Sirus, and V.A.S.T. Burchell’s drumming has the clipped exactitude of somebody who has spent years learning how machines think, while Rayner sings from inside the mess those machines could never clean up. Desire behaves like bad wiring in the skull, making sleeplessness feel necessary and self-erasure almost reasonable. The chorus grows huge enough to suggest somebody shouting through concrete, yet the verses keep dragging the listener back toward the private humiliation of knowing exactly what is happening and remaining unable to stop it. “I recently discovered the word ‘limerence’ and started thinking about extreme obsession,” says Rayner. “Hence the line “limerence closes every door” where no amount of reasoning can get through. Musically, it’s got dark, heavy riffs, cinematic synths and an epic chorus.” The video, directed by Lichen Sorrel and Rayner, places the band inside a rain-soaked environment where reality keeps slipping sideways. Their movements feel slowed and strangely detached, as though the performers have wandered into somebody else’s private hallucination and decided to finish the set anyway. Watch the video for Cease and Desist below: Rayner has been working toward this collision for decades. She began playing Australian pubs on bass at fourteen before moving into electronic production on an Atari computer, “which opened up a universe of creating sounds and moulding them into rhythms and melodies until they evoke the exact feeling I need.” Her history runs through Soulscraper, Sobriquet, Snog, and The Crystalline Effect before Robots In Love took shape in New Zealand in 2017. Joined by Burchell in this current powerhouse incarnation, the project has developed a nasty elegance that can turn technical precision into emotional damage. With second album OVERRIDE ahead and guitarist Henry Flynn Wall joining the record, Cease and Desist makes obsession feel less romantic than chemical, compulsive, and absurd in the terrible way our worst impulses often are. Love may open doors, but limerence bolts them shut from the inside. Listen to Cease and Desist below and pre-order OVERRIDE here. items.body: I’ll see you in the vacant light Somewhere in-between In a room that my body makes For you and me Some songs announce themselves with a manifesto. Violet Silhouette’s This Is Something seems perfectly happy admitting that nobody involved has quite figured out what the hell is happening yet. A chant catches against a taut backbeat, bass and drums immediately putting bodies in motion while the synthesizers maintain a cooler distance. There is some early Human League in that contrast between machine discipline and romantic uncertainty, while the repetitive rhythmic pull recalls LCD Soundsystem at their most economical. Violet Silhouette leave plenty of room around the beat, allowing repetition to become its own persuasive force. Five minutes later you may still have questions, although sitting down probably will not be among them. This Is Something catches the instant before certainty settles in: two people meeting somewhere between confession and possibility, with a dance beat underneath them and enough unanswered questions to keep things interesting. The song began with rhythm. According to the band, the drums and beat drove its development while melodies were tested until the track revealed its peculiar identity. Compared with much of their forthcoming album, VIVID(IS)DECAY, This Is Something leans further into dance music, though its lyrics occupy considerably less certain territory. With Lily Vile joining on bass, Violet Silhouette now operates as a trio, and that expanded physical presence suits material built so firmly around movement. The group formed in West Palm Beach in late 2019 and has since become geographically divided between South Florida and Austin. Distance has become part of their method rather than an impediment, with Dan and Zaii exchanging early ideas for VIVID(IS)DECAY beginning in 2024. Night provides the setting, but clarity remains elusive. Someone is trying to make sense of where they have been while simultaneously wondering whether knowing would accomplish anything useful. Desire can be detected before it can be understood; feelings exist before language catches up with them. There is hesitation throughout the verses, coupled with a growing willingness to let another person see what has previously remained private. Then Violet Silhouette introduce one of the song’s strongest images: two people meeting somewhere between recognizable states, inside a private room formed by the body itself. Suddenly This Is Something feels less like an evasive title and more like an admission. Whatever this connection is, somebody has finally acknowledged its existence. The accompanying video carries the uncertainty somewhere considerably stranger. Violet Silhouette initially perform inside gorgeous neo-film-noir compositions, bodies moving with the backbeat before strobes, abstract tableaux, and blurred recollections begin interrupting any comfortable sense of reality. “Visually, we drew from David Lynch’s Lost Highway,” says the band. “Our friend Roberto Badillo took our vision and ran with it — the result is sleek and visceral, like a gloved hand dragging desire across the table.” That glove fits. Watch the video for This Is Something below: Produced, mixed, and mastered entirely by Violet Silhouette, VIVID(IS)DECAY explores what the band calls Neuromanticism, their pursuit of truth and love through unstable identities, secret languages, and emotional dissolution. items.body: Na skale Nad wodą Czaruje melodią For thousands of years, human beings have imagined voices calling to us from beyond the known world. The siren may be one of our oldest attempts to give desire a body. She waits at the boundary between land and sea, reason and longing, safety and surrender. Her song has power because the sailor brings something to it: loneliness, hope, curiosity, the wish to discover what lies beyond the horizon. Perhaps this is why the legend survives. The danger has never been merely the siren. It is our extraordinary capacity to hear, in the vast and indifferent world, precisely what we most wish were calling our name. Dawid Walkusz’s Syrena begins with the patience of something seen from a great distance: a bass line moving heavily beneath the surface, drums keeping a measured pace, and guitars and synths spreading a pale haze around Julia Frycz’s voice. The arrangement, channeling Current Joys, Cocteau Twins, Motorama, and Slowdive, belongs loosely to post-punk, coldwave, dreampop, and hypnagogic pop; though its strongest quality is less categorical than physical. The song seems to advance through water, every beat slightly burdened, every melodic phrase suspended between sleep and recognition. Frycz, a visual artist and vocalist with Emrere, gives Syrena its strange center of gravity. Her singing carries the calm authority of a figure who already knows how the story ends. Walkusz had written the instrumental and recorded early vocal parts before Frycz joined him, yet the collaboration feels unusually unified, as though both musicians had been picturing the same coastline without realizing it. Their subject is the siren, familiar from folklore as an emblem of beauty sharpened into danger, and the Polish lyrics render her with almost childlike clarity: she sits upon a rock above the water, her eyes glint, she appears angelic, and beneath the surface waits a tail. This simplicity gives the song room to become stranger. Sailors are drawn toward her by longing and tenderness, losing their way before affection itself becomes fatal. Walkusz and Frycz avoid turning the myth into theatrical gothic excess. The menace comes from softness, from the slow reassurance of the voice and the bass line’s stubborn tread. Desire becomes a navigational error. Love becomes a current capable of carrying someone farther than intended. The accompanying video extends this idea along the seaside, where cairns, stones, and open water create a setting suspended somewhere between Romantic poetry and Pre-Raphaelite painting. Frycz appears among the rocks as the siren, recalling the doomed women of Waterhouse and the river-bound Ophelia of Shakespeare, while Maciej Cimaszkiewicz’s cinematography favors natural forms over elaborate staging. Walkusz, who handled the editing and post-production, worked closely with Frycz to preserve the same visual language that had developed around the song. The shoreline becomes a psychological border, a place where the familiar world thins out and the sailor’s attraction begins to resemble surrender. Watch Syrena below: Syrena is the first glimpse of Walkusz’s second solo album, Fantometyka, due in spring 2027, and it suggests a broader, more confident development from his debut, Monochrom. The earlier record established his attraction to austere rhythms and blurred textures; here, those elements have acquired a more sensual sense of space. The song moves slowly, almost ceremonially, and its danger lies in how comfortable that pace becomes. By the time the siren has finished singing, the sailor’s fate feels less like catastrophe than consent. Listen to Syrena below, and order the single here. items.body: Ten years is a long time to leave a monster in the basement, especially when you know it has been down there learning new tricks. Ghosts In The Graveyard return to their 2016 debut, Monsters For The Masses, with the zeal of directors who finally found the budget they wanted the first time around. Monsters For The Masses: Resurrected tears into the old recordings with fresh programming, heavier production, electronic detail, and the accumulated bad habits of a band that has spent a decade getting better at making darkness dance. The real kick comes from hearing Byron C. Miller’s younger self dragged into the present without sanding away the cheap-horror charm. Miller had just come out of eight years with God Module when the original record took shape, and you can still feel a frontman figuring out how much theater, electronics, guitar damage, and personal debris he could cram into his own clubhouse. “This album means the world to me,” gushes Miller. “After 8 years in God Module, this was the first music project I put together, the first time I was writing most of the lyrics, defining the aesthetic. The interludes on this album are made from cassette recordings I did when I was a little kid trying to be scary. In many ways these songs are the first half of my life as song. I’m so glad that my bandmate, music creator, Paul Morgan, was able to take everything he’s learned and go in and rebuild these tracks from the original recordings. I love how these new mixes were mastered by our pal, Chris Longo. This is how the album was always meant to sound!” Directed by Byron C. Miller and shot by cinematographer Paul Morgan, the Monster Mask video follows an eerie little vignette in which a woman’s peace is abruptly disturbed. We’ll leave the rest of the plot buried where it belongs, since spoiling horror is the cultural equivalent of telling somebody what is inside the coffin before they pry it open. One practical warning, however: the video contains extensive flashing lights, so viewers with photosensitivity should approach accordingly. Watch the video for Monster Mask: Resurrected below: Ghosts In The Graveyard know horror works best when somebody is having too much fun with it. “Better In Black: Resurrected Version” comes back with its teeth filed to fresh points, Paul Morgan rebuilding the track from the original masters while preserving the sleazy romantic pull that made it central to the band’s identity. Monster Mask: Resurrected Version sinks lower and stranger, bringing dark trip-hop tension into the graveyard. Then there is Debonair, the sole new recording, a cover of The Afghan Whigs that gives the project its best excuse for existing beyond anniversary bookkeeping. It has the heat of a band testing an old skeleton under stage lights, turning the album into a current document with ten years of dirt under its fingernails. Ghosts In The Graveyard still love blood, monsters, desire, death, and all the lurid furniture, yet the stronger point is how seriously they take the pleasure of performance. Resurrection becomes vandalism with better equipment, a chance to exhume their younger selves, hand them louder machinery, and see what starts moving. items.body: Oh how I want to love you Oh how I love to want you Oh how I love to hate you Oh how I hate to love you A persuasive EBM bassline can make almost any terrible proposition sound like it’s worth considering. Charm School’s Desolation makes the most of that weakness, setting a romance of taunts, submission, and calculated cruelty to a groove with suspiciously good manners. The invitation is easy to accept; the lyrics give you every reason to reconsider. The single pairs the Louisville-rooted, Los Angeles-based project with Matia Simovich of INHALT, who wrote the music, while Andrew Sellers, aka Andrew Charm, supplied the vocals and lyrics. It also serves as the lead single from a forthcoming EP that will include the late Steve Albini’s mix of Simulacra, Charm School’s first single. Matia Simovich of INHALT Simovich opens proceedings with a funky synth bassline, setting old-school synth stabs against drums intent on keeping the floor occupied. Metallic synth accents add a peculiar mechanical funk, their hard surfaces catching against the low end’s easy movement. There’s an EBM discipline to the arrangement and an Italo appetite for pleasure, with a trace of darkwave unease making itself comfortable between the two. Every sharp edge has something supple moving around it. Sellers attacks the vocal with a Stooges-era Iggy Pop drawl, mixed with the timbre and cadence of Lou Reed at his most forceful onstage. The compressed vocal sits prominently in the mix, with reverb sending the words ricocheting as though they were bouncing off sheet steel or passing through the blades of an industrial fan. That peculiar treatment gives each phrase a cold metallic afterimage. As the vocal develops, a bubbling synth figure lifts the groove, lending a playful buoyancy to a song whose romantic prospects are deteriorating by the line. The opening verse treats manipulation as a sales pitch, with a lover boasting of their dishonesty while angling to become the sole object of another person’s belief. By the second verse, that desire for control has tipped into a plea for surrender, even deception, as though being consumed by someone might offer its own peculiar relief. The roles seem to trade places, with domination and dependence feeding the same appetite. Images of kneeling, worship, and bodily sacrifice push the devotion toward something frighteningly absolute. The repeated title leaves that exchange with a bleak destination, while the closing permutations of wanting, loving, and hating keep rearranging the terms without resolving them. Each small change shifts the emotional balance. Pleasure survives in the music even as the words describe a relationship consuming itself, and the bassline keeps making its persuasive case for staying another few minutes. The collaboration also extends a connection dating back to our 2023 coverage of Simulacra, which credited Simovich with drum programming and noted alternate mixes by both Simovich and Albini. The forthcoming EP brings Albini’s version into the release plans alongside this new material, linking Charm School’s first statement to their latest electronic excursion. Listen to Desolation below and order the single here. Desolation by Charm School Sellers formed Charm School with longtime collaborators Matt Filip and Drew English, drawing on a Louisville upbringing steeped in Slint, Crain, and Rodan, alongside the catalogs of Touch & Go and Drag City. The disruptive instincts of PiL, Swell Maps, and The Fall sit beside an affection for Fugazi and Nation of Ulysses. Their debut EP, Finite Jest, appeared in July 2023, followed by the broader musical reach and acerbic satire of January 2025’s Debt Forever. This February’s Schadenfreude Ploy continued their examination of manipulation, tech wealth, and artificial intelligence. On Desolation, that interest in power finds an intimate setting, with two people apparently quite prepared to make each other miserable. items.body: Oh, holding on to yon and bitter falter Endless yearning weaves its web Among the forest, sheltered by her alter To be free, to be free Society of the Silver Cross draws on Gothic music’s old appetite for grand architecture, spiritual unease, and whatever might lie beyond ordinary daylight. Joe Reineke and Karyn Gold-Reineke built Temple of the Trees in Seattle, in part to accommodate that vision, filling the place with instruments that make a person wonder whether somebody has opened an archaeological dig beneath the control room. Their ongoing Temple Hymns series turns that studio into a meeting ground. Each installment brings another musician into the room to write and record with the pair, allowing personality, instinct, and whatever strange chemistry develops over several concentrated days to determine the results. Volume One brought in T.J. Cowgill of King Dude. For Temple Hymns Volume Two, Blood and Sun founder Luke Tromiczak flew from New York to Seattle and spent a week working with Reineke and Gold-Reineke. Tromiczak has led Blood and Sun since 2011, developing one of neofolk’s most recognizable baritones along the way. Put that voice beside twelve-string acoustic guitar, harmonium, B3 organ, Shahi Baaja, obscure synthesizers, and great booming toms and suddenly the room starts feeling considerably older than Seattle. Blood and Sun founder Luke Tromiczak Unraveled moves at the pace of somebody following a mountain trail after sunset with complete confidence that something significant waits at the other end. Its language circles freedom, transformation, lunar power, broken mirrors, concealed paths, and the promise of reunion. The arrangement carries the stateliness of Leonard Cohen into territory closer to Rowland S. Howard, while those deep drums suggest Ennio Morricone scoring some outlaw procession whose participants have traded revolvers for incense. The repetition in the vocal becomes nearly chant-like, working against the twelve-string guitar and organ until the track takes on a devotional character. Indian musical influence sits naturally beside American folk forms, giving the song an unusual spiritual geography. You can hear bits of Nick Cave, Nero Kane, and the Gun Club somewhere along the road, though everything has been dragged far enough into the Silver Cross universe to lose its passport. Battled Hands feels earthier, wounded by experience yet stubbornly pointed toward recovery in a call and response ballad. Tromiczak sings about endurance with the authority of somebody who understands that survival rarely comes accompanied by trumpets. Fire, dawn, damaged hands, storms, mercy, and returning light become markers along a long recovery from suffering. The slow progression allows each image enough room to settle before the drums push forward again. There is something almost physical about the weight of Tromiczak’s voice against the instrumentation. Reineke and Gold-Reineke surround him with enough space for every low note to feel carved into the room, while the harmonium and organ carry the devotional aspect further without turning the song into meaningless ceremony. Together, these two pieces make Temple Hymns Volume Two into a record of musicians discovering exactly how much ground they share. Listen to Temple Hymns Volume Two and order the double single here. Temple Hymns Vol. 2 by Society of the Silver Cross & Blood and Sun Society of the Silver Cross and Blood and Sun will take that meeting across Europe next month, where these songs should sound perfectly comfortable inside clubs, cellars, old halls, and any room willing to surrender its ordinary dimensions for a few minutes. items.body: There was always something faintly threatening about DEVO, even when they were dressed like escaped laboratory technicians and making middle America wonder whether Akron had been contaminated by industrial runoff. By 1984’s Shout, however, their absurdism had become so synthetically swollen that Puppet Boy could almost pass for another piece of mutant pop comedy. DEVO also have a long history of unconventional covers, from the classic Stones track I Can’t Get No Satisfaction, to Jimi Hendrix’s R U Experienced? Bex Delgado, recording as The Phantom Eyes, turns the tables on the Spud Boys: she hears the threat lurking inside Mark Mothersbaugh’s words and gives it a set of fangs. This version of Puppet Boy takes DEVO’s original premise and drags it into the bedroom of an especially disreputable vampire. The synthesizers feel colder and more severe, the rhythm carries a steady club-floor compulsion, and Delgado sings with the cool authority of somebody who already knows which end of the leash belongs in her hand. Mothersbaugh’s lyrics suddenly acquire an uncomfortable erotic logic. Obedience, dependency, affection, and ownership begin rubbing against one another until nobody seems especially interested in establishing boundaries. That change suits The Phantom Eyes remarkably well. Delgado approaches post-punk and dark electronic music through horror, where desire frequently comes with unfortunate contractual obligations and love can involve surrendering both your better judgment and access to daylight. There is humor inside it, too. Any cover of “Puppet Boy” that treats the title with complete solemnity would miss part of DEVO’s genetic code. Delgado preserves the perversity while turning the joke several degrees darker. The accompanying video makes the implication explicit. Filmed by Tori Kellogg/GR4VES in a single evening, it pairs Delgado’s scarlet entity with Sett’s Puppet Boy, a willing captive whose submission appears to have become his natural state. Red satin, CRT distortion, VHS degradation, and physical closeness give the footage the grubby glamour of an 80s vampire cassette discovered behind the counter of a video store that probably should have been investigated by local authorities. Some sequences were even filmed directly from Gr4ves’ CRT, giving the images their wonderfully diseased television texture. “I was trying to embody the spirit of not exactly a dom/sub relationship, but more like a master/servant one,” says Delgado. “This story isn’t romantic in nature, but still has that sweet feeling that the characters do take care of each other. I wanted the Puppet Boy to be not just a “sub,” but rather someone who just doesn’t really know anything else because it’s his whole life–and he has long been fine with this.” The Puppet Boy has no great awakening coming. He knows his place, perhaps enjoys it, and The Phantom Eyes leave him exactly where DEVO put him forty-two years ago: attached to invisible strings, smiling nervously, waiting for somebody else to pull. items.body: I’m a living god In the same way as all human flesh A pretty song can pose a problem when your band has spent a decade cultivating less agreeable habits. Melbourne quartet Bitumen found themselves facing precisely that predicament with “Perffect Dress,” a handful of chords that had begun behaving suspiciously well. Their response was to introduce a little trouble: vocal distortion, an outlaw-country inflection, and a bouzouki. Beauty survived the intervention, though its manners became considerably less predictable. The single offers an unexpected turn ahead of Reality Red, the band’s third album, due November 6 via It Records. Acoustic instruments and live drums open up fresh possibilities for a group whose post-punk has long accommodated goth, metal, and electronic abrasion. Here, that expansion takes the form of something loose-limbed and oddly pastoral, with a threat tucked into its Sunday best. A slow drum crash and twanging acoustic guitar set the pace, with further strings gathering around the opening figure. There is a country-folk lilt to the arrangement, carried by the easy movement of Andrew Huhtanen McEwan’s drums and Bryce Maher’s bouzouki. As the layers accumulate, a deep bass hum draws the music toward alternative rock and post-punk, while a high electric-guitar line swims through the spaces overhead. The song seems happy to wander, even as its low end keeps track of where everyone is going. Kate Binning’s voice gives that wandering its peculiar charm. Her vocal suggests Marianne Faithfull meets Thom Yorke’s languid reverie. The distortion adds texture without making the performance abrasive; there is an almost whimsical quality to the delivery, a daydream being sung aloud before anyone has checked its contents. Simon Maisch’s murmured backing vocals move beneath her, introducing a second, less easily deciphered train of thought. The words supply ample reason to inspect that daydream. Revenge, freeway exposure, pursuit, and the vulnerability of flesh run through lyrics that keep shifting between smallness and grandiosity. The speaker can be a little sound one moment and a living god the next, claiming divinity on the same terms as every other mortal body. Rearranging a perfect dress becomes a wonderfully incongruous gesture amid all this damage: a small adjustment to one’s appearance while existence itself appears to be coming apart. The overlapping vocal lines complicate the picture further, slipping bodily images and cryptic instructions beneath the lead. The accompanying video places the band around an open fire against corrugated metal, their faces and instruments catching its orange light. Rectangular close-ups overlap the wider performance, bringing hands on strings and Binning’s singing face into the foreground while the gathering continues behind them. As those frames change size and position, the clip moves between collective intimacy and private concentration. It suits the song’s peculiar hospitality: pull up a chair, enjoy the acoustic guitars, and try to overlook the revenge being discussed beside the flames. Watch the video for Perffect Dress below: ﻿ Formed in Melbourne in 2016, Bitumen brings together Kate Binning, Sam Varney, Bryce Maher, and Simon Maisch. Working with a drum machine has been a deliberate part of their approach, allowing guitars, synthesizers, samples, and programmed rhythms to change the terms of each song. On Reality Red, Tongue Dissolver’s McEwan adds live drums to that existing setup, while acoustic instrumentation and a greater openness to melody give the four-piece further room to experiment. Perffect Dress was recorded by Maisch at Lily Street Studios in Coburg North, with McEwan assisting, and produced by the band. Reality Red is available to pre-order here on digital and limited-edition transparent red vinyl through It Records. items.body: Curses Perfect High Altered Circuits Luca Venezia is a tastemaker DJ and producer in the classic mold; via his remixes, curation as the selector behind the superlative Next Wave Acid Punx compilations, and his releases CURSES, the Berlin based artist has been forging a varied, but consistent blend of darkwave, disco, EBM that keeps an eye to the dancefloor but doesn’t skimp on the atmosphere. On Perfect High Venezia digs deep into the new beat and NRG sounds that have informed his work, leaning heavily on funky rhythm programming for grooves. The title track doesn’t waste much time, establishing a big shuffling rhythm accented by orch hits, buzzy synth bass and stabs of sampled guitar to carry the track, its melody limited a simple repeating synth 3 note synth figure and repeated vocals. “Killer Instinct” strips everything down drums and e-bass, much of its texture found in the delay and reverb trails that follow its metallic perc hits and vocal samples. The new beat influence really comes to a head on “Dare 2 Dream”, where a brassy lead flies above pitched and chopped samples and a simple but effect kick-snare pattern, rolling hard at a dancefloor friendly mid-tempo rhythm. CURSES rarely misses, and given how in his wheelhouse Perfect High is, he wasn’t about to start here. Curses – Perfect High EP by Curses Transmigration Living Information self-released London act Transmigration has an immediate rush of nostalgic appeal on recent EP Living Information. Anyone cursorily familiar with electro-industrial will feel immediately at ease with the mix of echoing programming, samples, and vocals which reverberate through the title track or closer “Convergence” – a healthy balance of composition and production ensures that the acid panache of those tracks never oversteps the solid grooves at their base. But spend a bit more time with the EP and you’ll be impressed by how Transmigration’s able to call back to the antecedents of that style as well as bring it into the present without losing their own personality. “Ceaseless” carries a familiarly furtive 242 style forward via the like of Visitor and other modern lo-fi stylists, while the stuttering electro kicks of “Understanding” suggest either Kontravoid or (real heads remember) By Any Means Necessary. That’s a pretty wide historical spread, but Transmigration’s vocal personality as well as their yen for wet, dark electro reverb links those respective points along a thirty-plus year history quite handily. Fun, chewy, and satisfying listening for those who know their history. Living Information by Transmigration The post Observer: Curses & Transmigration appeared first on I Die: You Die.

items.body: I didn't really like Holocene. I could, however, appreciate it. That distinction is important: while the album wasn't for me, I could see what The Ocean were trying to do with it. More than that, I accepted that experimentation and change was the entire point of the project. Hell, Pelagial (still my favorite album from the band) is built around the very idea of change and transformation. But the direction the band was going in wasn't for me; I didn't think they executed it with enough skill to hold my interest. And so, I approached Solaris with some trepidation. I knew what to expect, namely something different, especially when I heard that four new band members were being added. What form would The Ocean take this time? Would some of the "old" sound return and, more importantly I think, did I want it to?Well, the answer to both of those questions is "sort of". Solaris is definitely more akin to Pelagial and Phanerozoic than Holocene was. It has plenty of electronic sounds and touches to it but it very much revolves around some of the tried and true elements of The Ocean, namely post-metal built around a concept album. But there are also differences. As you might be able to tell from looking at the cover art, Solaris is a "brighter" album. What do I mean by that? First, the compositions are less organized around crushing force and more around exploration and melody. Even Phanerozoic, which wasn't explicitly built around the concept of weight like Pelagial was, used its instruments to oppress and crush. But Solaris has a whole gamut of new sounds; check out "Light Pollution" for example and the undulating, mercurial segment around the four minute mark and especially the exquisite guitar bridge around four minutes and fifty seconds.Have you really heard The Ocean do this in the past? Not quite. And while you're there, you probably picked up on the vocals of Lane Shi (Elizabeth Color Wheel, Fórn) who is by far the biggest new addition to this album. The Loic Rosetti style vocals, which Enrico Tiberi does an uncanny job of recreating, really benefit from having a counter-part on this release. It's not that Tiberi's voice is boring. But the interaction between his timbre and the rest of The Ocean's instruments is tried and true. Shi, on the other hand, brings a whole new texture and palette to the record, creating much of that "brightness" I was referring to earlier. Whether screaming, vocalizing, humming, or emoting she's a breath of fresh air to the record and my favorite change on it by far. Other changes include those I've already highlighted, like new ideas from new guitarists, new ideas for how tracks are "stitched" together, like the bells on "Simulacra" or the overall approach to leitmotifs and guitar riffs on the album.Speaking about "Simulacra", holy shit do I love this track. It's perhaps my favorit example of what Solaris does so well. It's definitely The Ocean but it also sounds so different, the chords chosen, the structure of the track, the synths, even what Staps does with his singing on this track. It builds up to something much more exciting than just a retread. Rather, it's a rethink, an approach to the band's past that insists not just on regurgitation but a reprocessing that results in a new approach towards the same goal and sound. Which brings me back to the question of did I want the "old" The Ocean back and my answer of "sort of". I am very happy to hear the heaviness come back to the foreground and The Ocean back to what they do well: creating meticulously constructed, concept heavy post-metal. But I am also equally happy that they did not go back to Pelagial or Phanerozoic, as much as I love those releases. I am extremely glad that they held on to what I think makes them unique and yes, what sometimes leads them to make releases I don't enjoy as much: their fierce dedication to change. You never know what The Ocean will do next and they have proven this once again on Solaris. Thankfully, the end result is also something I love.

items.body: Top PickThe Ocean – Solaris (progressive post-metal) Eden should be along with a proper review sometime in the near future, but it's safe to say this first outing from the new Ocean line-up is not only a bona fide success, but also stands out as one of their strongest albums to date. The jump in quality might not come as a surprise after the snoozefest that was Holoxene (2023), but there's an argument to be made that this is the best Ocean album since genuine GOAT-contender Pelagial (2013), or even outside of it.At well over an hour and with songs and song-suites pushing the ten, fifteen and even twenty-minute mark, Solaris can be a tall order. Likewise, its expansive and layered composition works best when played in full and paying it complete attention, which is probably why I haven't listened to it nearly as much as I should have, even though we've had the promo for a month or so now. Rest assured though, that this is an album I will be playing and referring back to for years to come, and I doubt I'm alone in that assessment. Solaris by The Ocean Last Week's Most Unjustifiably Overlooked ReleaseUncle Acid and the Deadbeats – Shapes of Midnight (occult rock/metal)I didn't give this one a proper listen before posting last week's roundup, we got the promo early, but, after a quick sample I wrote it off as a good album from a band I respected but traditionally Wasn't For Me™. I should have paid more heed to Jordan's review though, because—while I'm not qualified to comment on whether this is the best Uncle Acid and the Deadbeats album—I can say its doing a whole lot more for me than any of their previous records have, or similar releases of its ilk have been lately.In comparison to the shark-jumping self-parody of the new Green Lung record, Shapes of Midnight oozes class and sincerity, along with a compelling mastery of its craft. It also rocks super hard. Along with the expected malaize of psychedelic Black Sabbath worship that pervades their sound, "Psycho on the Loose" sounds like Turbonegro covering Turbo-era Judas Priest, while "Don't Let it Control You" almost sounds like Motorhead mixed with Hellhammer, with lots of bass fills that bring to mind "Born to Be Wild". Indeed, bassist Justin Smith may well be the man of the match, delivering a Meddle-esque Pink Floyd trudge on "When Evil Wakes" and plenty of Geezer Butler-isms throughout that help make Shapes of Midnight a surprisingly vital pre-summer soundtrack as the weather starts to get warmer down under. items.body: 2026.09.25 奈良を拠点に、教育・海外展開・音楽祭へ 2026年に創設5周年を迎えたジャパン・ナショナル・オーケストラ（JNO）。9月16日に開催された記者会見では、代表を務める反田恭平がこれまでの歩みを振り返るとともに、6年目以降の活動について語りました。 JNOの前身は、2018年に反田恭平を中心に結成された「MLMダブル・カルテット」で、その後「MLMナショナル管弦楽団」へと発展。2021年5月に株式会社ジャパン・ナショナル・オーケストラが設立されました。DMG森精機の支援を受け、日本では初となる株式会社のオーケストラとして活動をスタートしています。 5年間の活動実績は、国内ツアー90公演、海外ツアー7公演、リサイタル・室内楽シリーズ90公演（いずれも2021～2025年）。2023年度からは3年連続で黒字となりました。 メンバーそれぞれが音楽家として広がった5年間 5年間を振り返り、反田が強調したのが、JNOのメンバーそれぞれの活動の広がりについてです。 「5年前、7年前、この仕事を始めた頃から、その当時は若手ですし、みんな学生だったんですけども、それが十人十色になって、自分で活動できるような面もあります」 JNOの活動と並行して、メンバーたちはソリストや室内楽奏者として、それぞれのキャリアを築いてきました。反田自身も、メンバーの演奏を聴くなかで成長を感じることがあるといいます。 その歩みは、国際コンクールでの結果にも表れています。2021年のショパン国際ピアノ・コンクールでは反田が第2位に入賞。その後も、岡本誠司がARDミュンヘン国際コンクールで第1位、水野優也がプラハの春国際音楽コンクールで第1位となるなど、JNOのメンバーは国内外で活動の場を広げています。 奈良で「成長の過程」をつくる もう一つ、JNOの5年間を語るうえで欠かせないのが、奈良を拠点とした活動です。2022年から奈良でのアウトリーチを本格化し、2025年には学校での演奏指導や街角演奏など、年間55回の活動を行ないました。また、奈良県立文化会館のリニューアルに向けたアドバイザーとしても活動しています。 奈良を拠点にする理由について、すでに多くのオーケストラが大きな都市で活動するなかで競争することとは異なる考え方があると説明しました。「奈良は、これから成長していく過程を一緒に見られる場所」。 今後は、2027年にリニューアルオープンする奈良県立文化会館を新たな活動拠点として、さらに地域との連携を深める計画です。 次の5年は「教育」「海外」「音楽祭」へ 6年目以降のビジョンとして発表されたのは、教育、配信・音源制作、海外展開、奈良県立文化会館、音楽祭の5つです。 教育面では、これまでのアウトリーチ活動をさらに発展させ、将来的なアカデミー設立を目指します。音源制作ではCDの制作に加え、ラジオや映像配信にも取り組みます。海外から指揮者やアーティストを招聘する計画もあり、2028～2029年ごろには音楽祭の始動も目指しています。 「今まで来てくださって、応援してくださっているこのオーケストラのファンの方々に、どういうふうにその恩返し、還元をできるかを考えていきたいと思います」 創設から5年。この先は演奏会だけにとどまらず、音楽家を育てる教育、奈良という地域との連携、海外との交流、音楽祭の開催へと活動領域を広げていきます。

ブランフォード・マルサリスとダイアン・リーヴス、Blue Noteでの再会 ブランフォード・マルサリス・カルテットと、ヴォーカリストのダイアン・リーヴスによるコラボレーションアルバム『Dedicated To You』が、Blue Noteからリリースされた（UK Supreme』を完全収録した経緯を持つ人物でもある。一方のダイアン・リーヴスは、10代の頃にクラーク・テリーからスタンダード・レパートリーの手ほどきを受け、1977年には「カルデラ」への参加を経て、1987年にBlue Noteと契約した最初の歌手となった歌い手である。系譜の異なる二人が同じ盤の上で言葉を交わす構図に、このアルバムの聴きどころがある。 出典：https://ukvibe.org/album_reviews/branford-marsalis-dianne-reeves ローランド・カーク、晩年の「新しさへの追求」 マルチリード奏者ローランド・カークの晩年の意欲作『Slightly Latin』が、Jazz Journal誌のコラム「JJ 09/66」で改めて取り上げられている。トロンボーン奏者ギャレット・ブラウンとの共同編成のもと、ラテン音楽の要素を取り込み、カーク特有の角ばった音色をより柔らかく響かせようとした一枚だという。 本作の背景には、1960年代半ばのジャズシーンにラテン音楽の語彙が浸透していった時期の空気がある。カークがバリトン・サックスという新たな声を得ようとしていたことも、Jazz Journalの評は伝えている。同誌はこの模索を「新しさへの絶えない追求」と評した。   出典：https://jazzjournal.co.uk/2026/09/20/jj-09-66-roland-kirk-slightly-latin アンディ・シェパード、静謐に寄せる5作目 イギリスのサックス奏者アンディ・シェパードの5作目となる新作『Salt Catchers』が、ECMから発表された（UK Jazz News）。出典によれば、本作は伝統に根ざした叙情性と、音数を絞った静けさを湛えた一枚だという。 シェパードは、ピアニストのリタ・マルコトゥッリ、ベーシストのミシェル・ベニータら長年の共演者と再びこの一枚を作り上げた。出典によれば、シェパード自身はキャラ・ブレイの「Lawns」をこれまでライブでは演奏してきたが録音してこなかったといい、今回初めて本作で録音に収めたという逸話も紹介されている。ここでは、シェパード個人がこの叙情性とどう向き合ってきたかという、小さな一点に絞って触れておく。 出典：https://ukjazznews.com/andy-sheppard-salt-catchers ジョーイ・アレクサンダー、10歳で世界に見出された歩み ジャズピアニスト、ジョーイ・アレクサンダーを取り上げた評論記事が『UK Jazz News』に掲載された。バリ島出身の彼は、2014年、10歳でニューヨークに移り住んだ直後にその演奏がウィントン・マルサリスの目に留まり、そこから国際的なジャズシーンへ足を踏み入れた経歴を持つ。 「アジア発のジャズプレイヤーが国際的に認識される時代」という大きな見立てを、今回の出典1件だけで裏づけるのは難しい。ここでは、一人のピアニストがどこから歩き出し、誰に見出されたかという個人史の線を辿るに留める。 出典：https://ukjazznews.com/joey-alexander コルトレーン生誕100年の節目に ジョン・コルトレーンが生まれてから、今年で100年になる。NPRのジャズ評論欄では、この節目に寄せた論考が公開されている（NPR、2026年9月22日）。 今回参照できた素材は表題と概要のみで、論考本文の具体的な主張までは確認できていない。テナー・サックス奏者としての革新性については、出典本文を確認できた段階で改めて扱いたい。 出典：https://www.npr.org/2026/09/22/nx-s1-5976887/marking-the-100th-birthday-of-jazz-great-john-coltrane 投稿 【ARBAN WEEKLY ／今週の話題まとめ】コルトレーン生誕100年、そしてブランフォードとリーヴスの邂逅ほか は ARBAN に最初に表示されました。

items.body: Music For Drifting is the debut LP from Aase Frejadóttir. Releasing on Editions Verde, and using synthesizers, field recordings, strings, and voice, Frejadóttir’s music isn’t afraid to switch things up. Straight off the bat, her music feels incredibly expansive while also remaining intimate and warm. There’s no doubt that the warmth is due to the synth, and it radiates from it, but its soft swells and the emergence of a new melody also helps to provide a benevolent atmosphere of awe and wonder that fits in with the warmer sound. Whether walking her dog, Pulsar, or drifting through the forests on the outskirts of Stockholm, Aase’s music appears to be a free spirit, in search of something more: extracting deeper meanings from the music, which is a glowing stream of distant light. A lover of Astronomy from an early age, Aase’s music is interwoven with the black fabric of space, containing material from an infinite beyond, and she builds her spacious music upon its bedrock – the glowing light of dead stars and something of the cosmic is audible in her music. Strings burst forth and a radiant harmony bursts onto the scene with the royal elegance, grace, and supreme force of a bejewelled supernova. Her music is constantly shifting, turning, its refractions and reflections rebounding and moving from note-to-note. Everything is tied to the Universe and the greater unknown, but although wide open arms and spatial possibilities are present on Music For Drifting, Aase never loses touch with what she and seven billion others call home, as heard in the more familiar, meteorological music of rain. That deluge of rain opens up ‘Dimma Promenad’, bringing us back to the soil and the earth, before transitioning into standout piece ‘Solemn Oath’ – twenty minutes of sweeping, orchestrated movements and patient drones. Cascading melodies glint and gently oscillate, and although the piece centres on a cluster of notes, it manages to evoke a ton of space and a reverential air fitting for a sacred oath. The notes are as pure and blessed as Holy Water. Following on is ‘Aerial’, which, with its additional layering, immediately counter-balances the previous piece. It favours depth over a skeletal fragility, and plump notes over a slimmer variant. Companionship and friendship over a solitary, long-forgotten corner of space, like the Earth’s positioning in the Milky Way. The mood is one of reflection and contemplation, not looking to figure things out with scientific equations or facts about the Universe, but rather revelling in its being. One can believe in the theory of an animated Universe when listening to her music. It’s enjoying existence for what it is: glorious, painful, tragic, thrilling. EV008: Music for Drifting by Aase Frejadóttir www.editionsverde.bandcamp.com

items.body: These original soundscapes – from anthéne, Slow Dancing Society, and orchestramaxfieldparrish – are a tribute to Joni Mitchell. Swallowed by the Sky, textura’s fourth release, is a homage to the singer-songwriter, revealing a deep appreciation for both person and music. Her legacy stretches far beyond any one genre or style, and while these aren’t covers – far from it – they channel her spirit. In some ways, they come closer to the truth of her music, touching meanings and lighting upon atmospheres in a deeper way. Covers can’t replicate that. While there are plenty of compilations and covers of her songs, there hasn’t been much, if anything, in the way of ambient. Such is her range, she’s inspired artists and musicians from all over the musical spectrum, going way into other stylistic fields and touching all different areas of music. Just as Jeff Stonehouse channelled the spirit of Mexico’s Chavela Vargas with his Listening Mirror release, On The Passing of Chavela, so too do these three ambient musicians dedicate their music to Joni, and in doing so, they evoke something just as deep as her soulful songs. This sweet, soothing music has a light, feminine touch, singing on the air like a wordless expression of her vocal poetry. Lyrics are huge in popular music, but music is so much more than that, and these instrumentals are able to delicately touch wider borders without the sweet entanglement of vocals. Brad Deschamps, Drew Sullivan, and Mike Fazio are all under her spell, and the music demonstrates a deep admiration and respect. The pieces also explore the light-and-dark juxtapositions in her songs. Lightness is eclipsed and replaced by a subtle change in mood, the sky becoming overcast and sullen; a changing of the times. The bass is an anchor, and melodies are allowed to blossom: the trio give their pieces sustenance and grounding, and, much like Joni’s songs, they come from a place deep down in the soul, given free roam to flower. SWALLOWED BY THE SKY by anthéne | Slow Dancing Society | orchestramaxfieldparrish www.textura.bandcamp.com

items.body: For this release on Canadian label caduc, Ryoko Akama, Cristián Alvear, Cyril Bondi, and d’incise perform Taku Sugimoto’s “mada”. The first section features pin-pricks of guitar punctuating controlled feedback, harmonium, and bowed metals, each instrument following its own line of single tones, but each modifying perceptions of the pitch, speed, and duration of all the others. Everything moves slowly, quietly. You have to slow down to catch these perceptions — slow down your thoughts, your heart rate, your expectations. Sometimes the tones may disappear completely, due to their own low volume, the masking of other noises in the environs, or your own mind racing ahead and losing the thread. You get the impression that’s ok though. The second section is five minutes of silence, while the third and final one picks up where the first left off, introducing piano and percussion in the place of harmonium and bowed metals. The slowly changing combinations of tones and timbres could be compared to a kind of topology: contours rising and falling in pitch and volume, creating undulating slopes, sharp peaks, and flat valleys of silence. To say that the sounds occur at random is like saying a landscape rises and falls at random. It may well appear that way to you given that you didn’t see the millennia of water and wind erosion that gave rise to the topology now before you; yet some sense of logic is still dimly intuitable, a logic that any geologist would be able to explain. ‘Mada’ means ‘still’ in Sugimoto’s native Japanese, and the stillness of the piece contributes to the landscape-like nature of each section. The performance recorded by Akama, Alvear, Bondi, and d’incise is entrancing, with well-chosen sounds combined with precise control and subtlety. Their deep understanding of the music and of each other’s playing makes what could have been a dull, shapeless exercise into an absorbing panorama of sound. In today’s compulsively frenetic and cacophonous world, stillness is as rebellious and counter-cultural as it is rare; the still contours of music such as “mada” reveal the flatness of everything else.     Taku Sugimoto Ryoko Akama Cristián Alvear Cyril Bondi d’incise caduc
